items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your Zustand store has a cards array inside each column. When a user renames a card, you update the store. How do you write the update function that changes one card's title inside a nested structure? Use immer or manual immutability: set(state => ({ columns: state.columns.map(col => col.id === columnId ? { ...col, cards: col.cards.map(card => card.id === cardId ? { ...card, title: newTitle } : card) } : col) })). Alternatively, install the immer middleware for Zustand: it lets you write set(produce(state => { state.columns.find(c => c.id === columnId).cards.find(c => c.id === cardId).title = newTitle })). Immer handles the immutability automatically.

mastery_questions: Your Zustand store has a cards array inside each column. When a user renames a card, you update the store. How do you write the update function that changes one card's title inside a nested structure? Use immer or manual immutability: set(state => ({ columns: state.columns.map(col => col.id === columnId ? { ...col, cards: col.cards.map(card => card.id === cardId ? { ...card, title: newTitle } : card) } : col) })). Alternatively, install the immer middleware for Zustand: it lets you write set(produce(state => { state.columns.find(c => c.id === columnId).cards.find(c => c.id === cardId).title = newTitle })). Immer handles the immutability automatically.

You add drag-and-drop. The dragover event fires hundreds of times per second as the user moves the card over a column. Updating Zustand state in dragover would cause hundreds of re-renders. How do you prevent this? Track the drag target with a ref rather than state: const dragTarget = useRef(null). Update the ref in dragover (dragTarget.current = columnId). Only update the Zustand store in the ondrop event, when the drag completes. Refs do not trigger re-renders — they are mutable containers that persist across renders. Use refs for frequently-changing values that should not trigger renders.

Your Kanban board loads the initial state from localStorage via Zustand persist. A user opens the board on a new device and gets an empty board. The localStorage on this device is empty. How do you handle the first-visit experience? The Zustand persist middleware reads from localStorage; if no saved state exists, it uses the initial state defined in the create function. Define a meaningful initial state: one or two default columns (To Do, In Progress, Done) with one sample card. The user sees a useful starting point rather than an empty board, which is especially important for understanding how to use the application.

You want to undo the last action (a common Kanban requirement). How do you implement undo with Zustand? Keep a history of states: an array of previous states. Before every action that modifies the board, push the current state to the history array. The undo action pops the last state from history and sets it as the current state. Limit history length to prevent unbounded memory growth. Zustand's temporal middleware (part of the zustand ecosystem) implements this pattern for you.

Your Kanban board has a keyboard shortcut: pressing 'n' when hovering over a column opens the add-card input. You implement this by tracking hovered column ID in the store. As the user moves the mouse, you update the hovered column ID in Zustand. The entire board re-renders on every mouseover. What is the wrong pattern here and how do you fix it? Frequently changing, non-data state (hover state, cursor position, drag target) should not live in the global Zustand store — it should live in local React state (useState) or refs within the component that uses it. The hovered column ID is UI state, not domain data. Putting it in the global store causes all store subscribers to re-render on every mouse movement. Use local useState in the Column component instead.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to help you design the Zustand store schema for the Kanban board. Describe all the data your board needs to store (columns, cards, their properties, any UI preferences) and ask it to suggest a TypeScript type for the store state. Discuss the tradeoffs of different schema choices — for example, whether to store columns as an array or as a map keyed by ID. Good schema design makes every feature easier to implement.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Your Stripe-integrated app's audience is paying customers. They expect: instant feedback, no broken flows, transparent pricing. A failed payment that loses their work = lost customer forever. Test the recovery flow as religiously as the happy path.
weeks.pre_flight: Install zustand: npm install zustand. Understand the Zustand create function: it takes a callback that receives set (to update state) and get (to read current state) and returns the initial state object. Know the drag-and-drop API: draggable attribute, ondragstart event (fires when drag begins), ondragover event (fires when dragging over a drop target — must call preventDefault to allow drop), ondrop event (fires when the drag is released on the target).
common_mistakes: Using Zustand for all state including ephemeral UI state. Zustand is for shared, persistent application state. Form input values, hover states, open/closed menu states — these belong in local useState. Over-centralising state makes components harder to reuse and understand.

Not splitting the Zustand store into slices for large applications. A single 500-line store becomes hard to maintain. Use Zustand's slice pattern: create separate files for each domain (cards, columns, UI state) and combine them.

Reading the entire state in a component subscription: useStore(state => state) causes re-renders on any state change. Always select the minimal slice: useStore(state => state.columns[columnId].cards). Only changes to that specific slice trigger re-renders of the subscribing component.

Not handling the case where the persisted state shape is incompatible with the current code. After adding new fields to your store schema, existing localStorage data from previous versions will be missing those fields. Add a version number to the persist config and a migration function that handles old state shapes.

Forgetting to call event.stopPropagation() in drop zone handlers. If your drop zones are nested (a card can be dropped on a card or on a column), the drop event can bubble up from the card to the column, triggering both handlers. Use stopPropagation to prevent this.
weeks.debug_help: The most confusing drag-and-drop bug is "the card drops to the wrong position." Debug by logging the source card ID and target column ID in the drop handler. Common causes: (1) the dragged item's ID is not being correctly passed through the drag events (use event.dataTransfer.setData and getData), (2) the drop target is a child of the intended column rather than the column itself — use event.currentTarget instead of event.target to get the element the listener is attached to, (3) the ondragover handler is not calling event.preventDefault(), which is required to allow drops.
stretch: Add card filtering: a search input above the board that filters cards across all columns to show only cards whose title or description matches. Implement using a Zustand selector that derives the filtered board state from the full state and the search query.

Implement board sharing via URL: encode the entire board state as a base64-encoded JSON parameter in the URL. A user can share the URL and the recipient gets the same board. Handle the case where the URL state is malformed.

Add card due dates and a "overdue" indicator: cards with a past due date show a red border. Implement automatic status updates: a card whose due date passes while the browser tab is open should update its visual state without a user action.

weeks.title: Node.js, Express, and the Server Side of JavaScript
weeks.context:
The browser runs JavaScript. The server is separate — a different process, often on a different machine, that receives HTTP requests and sends responses. Node.js lets you write server-side JavaScript with the same language you use in the browser, but the environment is completely different: no window object, no DOM, no localStorage. Instead, you have access to the filesystem, environment variables, databases, and the ability to listen for incoming HTTP requests.

Express is the minimal web framework for Node.js. Where Next.js is opinionated and full-featured, Express is a thin layer over Node's HTTP server that adds middleware (functions that process requests and responses), routing (mapping URLs to handler functions), and nothing else. Understanding Express means understanding how web servers work at the HTTP level, without framework magic hiding the details.

The URL shortener you build has one real engineering challenge: generating short codes. A 7-character alphanumeric code from a 62-character alphabet (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) gives 62^7 = 3.5 trillion possibilities — more than enough. But the codes must be unique. The two approaches are random generation with collision checking (generate a code, check if it exists in the database, retry if it does) and counter-based encoding (encode the auto-incrementing row ID as base62). The counter approach is simpler and has no collision risk.

TypeScript on the server is the same TypeScript you use in the browser — the same type system, the same compiler — but the types describe server-specific things: request bodies, response schemas, database row types. Defining these types explicitly catches entire categories of bugs before they reach production. A handler that expects req.body.url to be a string and receives undefined instead will throw a runtime error. A TypeScript type catching that discrepancy catches it at compile time.

The redirect endpoint is the product. When someone visits your short URL (e.g., short.ly/abc1234), your server looks up the code in the database, increments the click count, and responds with an HTTP 301 redirect to the original URL. The browser follows the redirect transparently. The entire user experience is seamless — they just end up at the destination.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your Express route POST /shorten receives a JSON body with a url field. You call req.body.url without any validation. What risks does this create and how do you address them? (1) req.body.url might be undefined (request body is malformed or the field is missing), causing a runtime error when you try to use it. (2) It might be a string but not a valid URL (e.g., "javascript:alert('xss')" — a protocol that can execute code when used as a redirect target). (3) It might be a very long string that overloads your database. Fix: use Zod or express-validator to parse and validate the request body before using it. Check that url is a string, parse it with new URL(url) to verify it is a valid URL, check the protocol is http or https, and enforce a maximum length.

mastery_questions: Your Express route POST /shorten receives a JSON body with a url field. You call req.body.url without any validation. What risks does this create and how do you address them? (1) req.body.url might be undefined (request body is malformed or the field is missing), causing a runtime error when you try to use it. (2) It might be a string but not a valid URL (e.g., "javascript:alert('xss')" — a protocol that can execute code when used as a redirect target). (3) It might be a very long string that overloads your database. Fix: use Zod or express-validator to parse and validate the request body before using it. Check that url is a string, parse it with new URL(url) to verify it is a valid URL, check the protocol is http or https, and enforce a maximum length.

You use the base62 encoding approach to generate short codes. The first URL gets code "0000001", the second gets "0000002". This reveals your usage volume (competitors can count your URLs by watching the codes). What is the downside of the random generation approach? Random generation requires checking for collisions — generating a code, querying the database to verify it does not already exist, and retrying if it does. At low volume, collisions are rare (birthday paradox: at 1 million URLs, the collision probability for a 7-char base62 code is still very low). At high volume, collision checking adds database reads. A middle path: start with counter-based encoding, apply a reversible integer bijection to scramble the number before encoding (this preserves uniqueness while making codes appear random).

Your redirect endpoint needs to look up a short code in SQLite and redirect. The lookup must be fast because every redirect adds latency to the user's navigation experience. What database optimisation makes lookups fast? An index on the short_code column. Without an index, SQLite scans every row to find the matching code — O(n) with n rows. With an index (CREATE INDEX idx_short_code ON urls(short_code)), lookups are O(log n) — a tree traversal through the B-tree index. The index must be created when the table is created, not after it grows to millions of rows (indexing an existing large table is expensive but necessary).

Your API returns errors as plain text strings ("Error: URL not found") from some endpoints and as JSON from others. Why is inconsistent error format a problem? Clients cannot reliably parse errors. A frontend that parses errors as JSON crashes when it receives plain text. An API gateway that inspects error messages expects a consistent format. Always return errors in the same format: { "error": "URL not found", "code": "NOT_FOUND" }. Document the error format in your API documentation and enforce it in every error handler.

You want to add rate limiting to your POST /shorten endpoint to prevent abuse. How do you implement this in Express? Use the express-rate-limit middleware: const limiter = rateLimit({ windowMs: 15 * 60 * 1000, max: 100 }); router.post('/shorten', limiter, shortenHandler). This limits each IP to 100 requests per 15-minute window. For authenticated users, use their user ID rather than IP as the identifier. Add informative response headers: X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset — these tell clients how many requests they have left and when the limit resets.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to help you design the database schema for the URL shortener. Describe all the data you need to store (short code, original URL, creation date, click count, user ID for future auth) and ask it to write the SQL CREATE TABLE statement with appropriate column types and constraints. Then write the TypeScript type that mirrors the database row. Schema design is the most consequential decision in this project — the schema you define now affects every feature you add in the coming weeks.
weeks.pre_flight: Install express, typescript, ts-node-dev, and better-sqlite3. Create a tsconfig.json with "module": "commonjs" and "target": "ES2020". Know what middleware is in Express: a function with signature (req, res, next) that processes the request before it reaches the route handler. Know what HTTP 301 and 302 redirects do: they tell the browser to go to a different URL. 301 is permanent (browser caches it), 302 is temporary (browser does not cache it).
common_mistakes: Not using express.json() middleware. By default, Express does not parse request bodies. You must add app.use(express.json()) before your routes to enable JSON body parsing. Without it, req.body is undefined.

Returning sensitive database errors to clients. If a database error leaks a stack trace or SQL query to the client, it reveals implementation details and potential vulnerabilities. Catch all database errors, log them server-side, and return generic error messages to clients.

Not using async/await correctly in Express route handlers. Express does not catch async errors by default. If your async handler throws, Express does not catch the rejection and the request hangs or crashes the process. Wrap async handlers: const asyncHandler = (fn) => (req, res, next) => Promise.resolve(fn(req, res, next)).catch(next). Or use the express-async-errors package.

Storing passwords or API keys in the SQLite database as plain text. Even in this early project, establish the correct habit: hash passwords with bcrypt before storing, store API keys in environment variables, never log sensitive values.

Not closing the SQLite connection properly. better-sqlite3 uses synchronous operations and does not require connection pooling, but closing the connection on process exit prevents data corruption: process.on('exit', () => db.close()).
weeks.debug_help: The most common Express TypeScript error is "Cannot find module 'express'" or "Module not found" even though express is installed. This usually means the TypeScript compiler is not finding the type definitions. Install @types/express as a dev dependency. If the error persists, check your tsconfig.json — moduleResolution should be "node" or "bundler". Also confirm that ts-node-dev (or tsx) is being used to run the server, not plain node (which does not understand TypeScript).
stretch: Add a click analytics endpoint: GET /stats/:code returns the number of clicks, the click timestamps, and a breakdown of referring domains (parsed from the Referer header logged on each redirect). This is the start of the analytics dashboard.

Implement custom short codes: allow users to specify their own code (e.g., "my-repo" instead of "abc1234"). Validate that the custom code only contains alphanumeric characters and hyphens, does not conflict with reserved paths (/api, /health, /stats), and is not already taken.
Add a link expiry feature: optional expires_at field. Redirect requests for expired links return a 410 Gone response with an informative message rather than a 404.

weeks.title: PostgreSQL, Prisma, and Designing Data You Won't Regret
weeks.context:
SQLite was right for getting started — zero configuration, single file, no server to manage. But it has real limits: no concurrent writes (only one writer at a time), no network access (the database must be on the same machine as the application), and limited tooling for production management. PostgreSQL is the production database that most web applications use. This week you migrate your URL shortener from SQLite to PostgreSQL and add Prisma as the ORM.

Prisma is an ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) that provides three things: a type-safe query client, a schema definition language, and a migration system. The schema (schema.prisma) is the single source of truth for your database structure. Prisma generates TypeScript types from it and generates migration SQL from it. When you add a field, you add it to the schema and Prisma generates the ALTER TABLE migration. You never write migration SQL by hand.

Database design deserves more attention than most beginners give it. The decisions you make now — table names, column types, nullability, foreign key constraints, indexes — are hard to change after the application is running with real data. The URL shortener has two main entities: Url (the link record with short code and original URL) and Click (each redirect event). The relationship is one-to-many: one URL has many clicks. How you model this relationship, what indexes you create, and how you handle deletion cascades all affect query performance and data integrity.

Prisma migrations are the mechanism that applies schema changes to the database safely. In development, prisma migrate dev generates and applies a new migration. In production, prisma migrate deploy applies pending migrations without prompting. The migration history is stored in the prisma/migrations directory and committed to git — this is the database's version history, analogous to git commits for code.

Connection pooling is the production concern that SQLite never required. PostgreSQL connections are expensive — establishing a new connection takes 50-100ms. An application that creates a new connection per request cannot handle significant traffic. Prisma manages a connection pool automatically, reusing connections across requests. The pool size is configurable: too small and requests queue waiting for a connection, too large and you hit PostgreSQL's maximum connections limit.
topics: Postgres fundamentals — tables, columns, types, primary keys, foreign keys
Schema design — normalisation vs denormalisation, when to break the rules
Indexes — B-tree, GIN, partial, when each helps, when they hurt writes
Transactions and isolation levels — what 'serialisable' actually means
Prisma — the schema file, generator, client, migration workflow

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You add a userId field to your Url model but mark it as optional (userId Int?). Later you decide every URL must have a user and change it to required (userId Int). Why can you not just change the schema and run a migration without extra steps? The migration would add a NOT NULL constraint to a column that already has NULL values (existing URLs created before auth was added). PostgreSQL rejects NOT NULL constraints on columns with existing NULL values. You must first fill in the NULL values — either by adding a default value (userId Int @default(1)), writing a migration that updates existing rows with a placeholder user ID, or accepting a two-step migration: add a temporary default, apply the constraint, remove the default. Database migrations on production data require careful planning.

mastery_questions: You add a userId field to your Url model but mark it as optional (userId Int?). Later you decide every URL must have a user and change it to required (userId Int). Why can you not just change the schema and run a migration without extra steps? The migration would add a NOT NULL constraint to a column that already has NULL values (existing URLs created before auth was added). PostgreSQL rejects NOT NULL constraints on columns with existing NULL values. You must first fill in the NULL values — either by adding a default value (userId Int @default(1)), writing a migration that updates existing rows with a placeholder user ID, or accepting a two-step migration: add a temporary default, apply the constraint, remove the default. Database migrations on production data require careful planning.

You want to get a URL and the count of its clicks in a single query. How do you write this in Prisma? Use include with _count: const url = await prisma.url.findUnique({ where: { shortCode }, include: { _count: { select: { clicks: true } } } }). This returns the URL record plus clicks: { _count: { clicks: 42 } }. Alternatively, use select with aggregate: prisma.url.findUnique({ where: { shortCode }, select: { shortCode: true, originalUrl: true, clicks: { select: { id: true } } } }). For high-read operations, store the click count as a denormalised field on the URL record and increment it on each click — this avoids a JOIN but requires careful consistency management.

Your Prisma query is slow: finding URLs by userId when a user has thousands of URLs. What do you add to fix this? An index on the userId field: @@index([userId]) in the Prisma schema. Prisma generates the corresponding CREATE INDEX migration. Without the index, PostgreSQL scans all URL rows to find those with the matching userId. With the index, the query uses a B-tree lookup. Index selection is critical: index columns that appear in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, and ORDER BY clauses. Too many indexes slow down INSERT and UPDATE operations (each index must be updated), so index selectively.

You delete a User and want all their URLs deleted automatically. How do you configure this in Prisma? Add a cascade delete: in the Url model, the user relation should have @relation(onDelete: Cascade). This tells PostgreSQL (via Prisma's migration) to automatically delete all Url rows when the referenced User row is deleted. Without this, deleting a User with existing URLs throws a foreign key constraint violation. Consider the alternative: a soft delete pattern where users are marked inactive rather than deleted, preserving historical data.

You want to run a raw SQL query in Prisma for a complex aggregation that Prisma's query builder cannot express efficiently. How? Use prisma.$queryRaw: const results = await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT DATE_TRUNC('day', created_at) as day, COUNT(*) as clicks FROM "Click" WHERE url_id = ${urlId} GROUP BY day ORDER BY day`. The tagged template literal automatically parameterises values, preventing SQL injection. Use raw queries sparingly — they bypass Prisma's type safety and do not benefit from query validation. But complex analytics queries often require raw SQL.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to help you write the Prisma schema for a feature beyond the basic URL shortener — for example, a team/organisation model where multiple users can share URLs. Describe the entities and relationships, ask it to draft the Prisma schema, and discuss the design decisions: why certain fields are optional, what the delete cascade strategy should be, which indexes are needed. This is the type of schema design discussion that normally happens in architecture reviews.

weeks.pre_flight: Install PostgreSQL locally (or use Neon, a free serverless Postgres provider). Install prisma and @prisma/client: npm install prisma @prisma/client. Run npx prisma init to create the schema file. Know the Prisma schema syntax: model Url { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()); shortCode String @unique; ... }. Know the difference between prisma migrate dev (creates and applies a new migration) and prisma migrate deploy (applies pending migrations without creating new ones).
common_mistakes: Instantiating a new PrismaClient on every request. Each PrismaClient manages a connection pool. Creating a new one per request creates hundreds of database connections. Instantiate PrismaClient once and export the singleton: export const prisma = new PrismaClient().

Not handling Prisma's "Record not found" error (P2025). findUnique returns null when no record matches, but update and delete throw P2025 when the record does not exist. Wrap these calls in try/catch and check error.code === 'P2025'.
Committing the DATABASE_URL to git. The database URL contains credentials. Store it in .env and add .env to .gitignore. Provide a .env.example file with the variable name but no value.

Running prisma migrate dev in production. migrate dev is for development — it can create and delete databases, prompt interactively, and create shadow databases. Production deployments should always use prisma migrate deploy, which only applies pending migrations without any destructive operations.

Not understanding Prisma's transaction API. If two database operations must succeed or fail together (create a URL and log the creation event), wrap them in prisma.$transaction([prisma.url.create(...), prisma.event.create(...)]). Without a transaction, one operation can succeed while the other fails, leaving the database in an inconsistent state.
weeks.debug_help: The most common Prisma error is "Cannot connect to database server at localhost:5432." This usually means PostgreSQL is not running locally. Start PostgreSQL with pg_ctl start or through the PostgreSQL app. If using Neon or another cloud provider, verify the DATABASE_URL in your .env matches the connection string from the provider dashboard (including the database name, username, password, and host). Add ?connection_timeout=30 to the connection string if connections are timing out before being established.
stretch: Add full-text search to URLs: allow searching by original URL and custom alias. Use PostgreSQL's full-text search (tsvector and tsquery) via Prisma raw queries. Compare the performance against a LIKE %search% query.

Implement cursor-based pagination for the user's URL list: instead of OFFSET-based pagination (which degrades at high page counts), use the last URL's ID as the cursor for the next page. This scales linearly regardless of page depth.

Build a database backup script that dumps the PostgreSQL database to a compressed file and uploads it to an S3 bucket. Schedule it with a cron job or GitHub Actions scheduled workflow. Test the restore process.

weeks.title: REST API Design — Endpoints People Don't Hate
weeks.context:
REST is not a technology — it is a set of constraints on how you use HTTP. The word "RESTful" is widely abused. What it actually means in practice: your API uses nouns (resources) not verbs in URLs, HTTP methods carry the semantic meaning of the operation, and responses use standard HTTP status codes so clients do not have to parse error messages to know what happened.

URL design: use plural nouns for collections (/users, /orders, /products). Use the pattern /resource/:id for individual items. Nest sub-resources when the relationship is ownership: /users/:id/orders means the orders that belong to a specific user. Do not nest more than two levels deep — it becomes unwieldy. Avoid verbs in URLs: /users/:id/delete is wrong; DELETE /users/:id is correct. The method IS the verb.

HTTP methods and their contracts. GET is safe (reading does not change state) and idempotent (calling it twice has the same effect as calling it once). PUT replaces an entire resource — sending PUT /users/1 with a partial body should fail or overwrite missing fields with null. PATCH updates specific fields only. POST creates a new resource or triggers an action; it is neither safe nor idempotent. DELETE is idempotent — deleting a resource that does not exist should return 404 or 204, but a second DELETE should not crash.

Status codes. 200 OK, 201 Created (after a successful POST), 204 No Content (success with no response body, common for DELETE). 400 Bad Request (malformed request body), 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict (duplicate email on registration), 422 Unprocessable Entity (valid JSON but failed validation). 500 Internal Server Error (something broke on the server). Never return 200 with an error message in the body — that makes your API a lie.

This week you design and build the full REST API for Bean Forge: CRUD endpoints for menu items, orders, and customers. You write an OpenAPI spec for it. You use zod for request validation so bad input never reaches your database.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You are designing an API for a blog. A user can like a post. What is the correct REST endpoint for this operation and why? The resource is the "like" relationship between a user and a post. The endpoint is POST /posts/:id/likes with the authenticated user's ID inferred from the JWT. To unlike, it is DELETE /posts/:id/likes/:userId. The wrong approach is POST /posts/:id/like-post — that uses a verb in the URL and is not idempotent. The right design models the like as a resource that can be created and destroyed.

mastery_questions: You are designing an API for a blog. A user can like a post. What is the correct REST endpoint for this operation and why? The resource is the "like" relationship between a user and a post. The endpoint is POST /posts/:id/likes with the authenticated user's ID inferred from the JWT. To unlike, it is DELETE /posts/:id/likes/:userId. The wrong approach is POST /posts/:id/like-post — that uses a verb in the URL and is not idempotent. The right design models the like as a resource that can be created and destroyed.

Your API endpoint POST /orders returns 200 OK with {"success": true} on success and {"success": false, "error": "Item out of stock"} on failure. What is wrong with this? The problem is that the HTTP status code always says 200, meaning "everything is fine." Clients (and monitoring tools, load balancers, and API gateways) use the HTTP status code to determine whether a request succeeded. A 200 with an error payload is invisible to infrastructure. A stock error should return 409 Conflict or 422 Unprocessable Entity with a structured error body. The status code is the contract — honour it.

You have a PUT /users/:id endpoint. A client sends a request with only {"email": "new@example.com"} — no name, no other fields. What should happen? PUT semantics say the entire resource is replaced by the request body. If name is not in the body, the correct behaviour is to set name to null (or the column default). If you want partial updates, the correct method is PATCH. Many APIs get this wrong and treat PUT as PATCH. The distinction matters because it changes client behaviour — PUT assumes the client has the full resource, PATCH assumes it only has the delta.

You add zod validation to your POST /orders endpoint. The schema requires quantity to be a positive integer. A client sends quantity: "5" (a string). How does this behave? Zod's .number() will reject the string "5" — it does not coerce by default. Use z.coerce.number().int().positive() if you want to accept "5" from a form submission (where all values are strings). Use z.number().int().positive() if you are a JSON API where strings are always wrong. Know which you need: JSON APIs should reject "5" because the client is sending the wrong type. Form handlers often need coercion because HTML forms cannot send typed values.

Understand what idempotent means: f(f(x)) = f(x). Understand what safe means in HTTP: the operation has no side effects.
common_mistakes: Returning 200 for errors. If something fails, return the appropriate 4xx or 5xx status. Clients check the status code first — they should not have to parse the body to know if the request succeeded.

Nesting routes too deeply. /users/:userId/orders/:orderId/items/:itemId is hard to work with. Flatten when the sub-resource makes sense on its own: /order-items/:id is fine if you can access items directly. Nest only when the parent ID is required for the operation.

Missing validation on all inputs. Validation only on the happy path is not validation. Validate that :id params are valid UUIDs or integers. Validate query parameters (page, limit). Validate request bodies. Reject early — do not let garbage reach your database layer.

Exposing database errors to clients. If Prisma throws a unique constraint violation, do not return the raw Prisma error message — it exposes your database schema. Map database errors to appropriate HTTP responses: unique constraint = 409 Conflict, foreign key violation = 400 Bad Request.

Using GET requests for operations that change state. GET /users/1/delete is wrong on two levels: verbs in URLs and a safe method used for a mutation. Browsers and caches may prefetch or cache GET requests. Mutations must use POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE.
weeks.debug_help: Request fails with 404 but the route exists: check the route registration order in Express — more specific routes must come before wildcard routes. Also check whether you are mounting a router with a prefix that changes the full path. Response says "Cannot POST /api/orders" (not your 404): the route is not registered at all, or the HTTP method is wrong. Use app._router.stack to list registered routes during debugging. Zod validation error returns a 500 instead of 400: you are not catching the ZodError. Wrap your validation in a try/catch and return 400 with z.ZodError.errors when validation fails. Prisma throws "Unique constraint failed" but you are catching it as a generic Error: check the error code. Prisma throws PrismaClientKnownRequestError with code P2002 for unique constraint violations. Check error.code before deciding on the HTTP status.
stretch: Add cursor-based pagination to your GET /menu-items endpoint. Return a cursor field in the response that the client can pass as a query param to get the next page. Offset-based pagination breaks when items are inserted during pagination — cursor-based does not.

Generate a Postman collection from your OpenAPI spec using the openapi-to-postman library and import it into Postman. Run the full collection and verify every endpoint returns the expected status codes.

Implement API versioning via URL prefix (/api/v1/...). Add a v2 endpoint that returns a different response shape for one resource. Think about how you would handle deprecation — add a Deprecation response header to v1 endpoints.

weeks.title: Authentication and Authorization — Done Right
weeks.context:
Authentication is about identity: who are you? Authorisation is about permission: what are you allowed to do? These are different systems and conflating them causes security holes. This week you build both correctly for Bean Forge, and you understand the tradeoffs between the two main approaches: sessions and JWTs.

Sessions: when a user logs in, you create a server-side session record (stored in a database or Redis) and set a session ID in an HttpOnly cookie. On every subsequent request, the browser sends the cookie, you look up the session, and you know who the user is. Sessions are easy to invalidate: delete the record. The cookie is HttpOnly so JavaScript cannot read it, preventing XSS token theft. The downside: every request hits the database. For most apps, this is fine.

JWTs (JSON Web Tokens): you sign a payload (user ID, roles, expiry) with a secret key and send the token to the client. The client stores it and sends it with every request. You verify the signature without hitting the database — stateless. The downside: you cannot invalidate a JWT until it expires. If a user's permissions change or their account is compromised, the old token keeps working until expiry. Workarounds exist (blocklist, short expiry + refresh tokens) but they add complexity. Use sessions unless you have a specific reason for JWTs (microservices, third-party clients).

Password storage: hash with bcrypt or argon2. Never store plain text. Never use MD5 or SHA-1 for passwords — these are fast hashing algorithms and can be brute-forced. Bcrypt is deliberately slow. The cost factor (work factor) controls how slow — a cost factor of 12 means 2^12 iterations. Always hash on the server — never trust a hash sent from the client.

OAuth 2.0: the protocol that powers "Sign in with Google." The user is redirected to Google, they grant permission, Google redirects back with an authorization code, your server exchanges the code for tokens using a back-channel request. The key security feature: the client secret never leaves your server. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) prevents code interception attacks when the redirect target is a public client (like a mobile app or SPA) that cannot keep a client secret.

This week: add email/password auth to Bean Forge with sessions. Add "Sign in with Google" using NextAuth or a manual OAuth implementation. Protect routes with middleware that checks for a valid session.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user logs in and you create a session. Two hours later, the user's account is suspended by an admin. The user still has their session cookie. What happens on their next request, and how do you handle it? The session lookup finds the session record in the database. But before trusting it, you must re-fetch the user from the database to check their current status. If you only store the user object in the session at login time, you will not see the suspension until the session expires. The correct approach: store only the userId in the session, fetch the user on every request (or cache with short TTL), and check the active/suspended status.

mastery_questions: A user logs in and you create a session. Two hours later, the user's account is suspended by an admin. The user still has their session cookie. What happens on their next request, and how do you handle it? The session lookup finds the session record in the database. But before trusting it, you must re-fetch the user from the database to check their current status. If you only store the user object in the session at login time, you will not see the suspension until the session expires. The correct approach: store only the userId in the session, fetch the user on every request (or cache with short TTL), and check the active/suspended status.

You want to implement "remember me" functionality — the session should last 30 days if the user checks the box, and 1 hour if they do not. How do you implement this? Set the session maxAge differently based on the checkbox. If remember me is checked: maxAge: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 (30 days in ms). If not: maxAge: 60 * 60 * 1000 (1 hour). The session store must also honour the expiry — connect-pg-simple deletes expired sessions. The cookie rolling option (re-setting maxAge on each request) prevents active users from being logged out.

You are implementing OAuth with Google. A user clicks "Sign in with Google", gets redirected, and Google returns them to your callback URL. How do you prevent a CSRF attack on the callback? The state parameter. Before redirecting to Google, generate a random string, store it in the user's session, and pass it as the state query parameter in the redirect URL. When Google returns to your callback, verify that the state parameter matches what you stored. If they do not match, reject the request. This prevents a malicious site from sending a user to your callback URL with an authorization code it obtained elsewhere.

Your login endpoint accepts {"email": "...", "password": "..."} and returns a session cookie. How do you prevent timing attacks that allow an attacker to determine whether an email address exists? Bcrypt's compare function takes roughly the same time regardless of whether the hash matches. But if the email does not exist, you skip the compare entirely — returning faster, which leaks that the email is not registered. Fix: always call bcrypt.compare even when the user is not found. Pass a dummy hash when the user is not found. This ensures the response time is consistent whether or not the email exists.
ai_assist: "Write a bcrypt-based email/password login function in TypeScript. It takes email and password, looks up the user in a Prisma database, compares the password hash, and returns the user or throws a specific error (not a generic one) for email not found vs wrong password. Use constant-time comparison to prevent timing attacks."

"I'm implementing OAuth with Google using the authorization code flow manually (not NextAuth). Give me the exact sequence: redirect URL construction, callback handler, token exchange, user upsert. Include the state parameter for CSRF protection."

"Write an Express middleware function that reads the session, fetches the current user from the database, checks that the user is active (not suspended), and attaches the user to req.user. Return 401 if no session, 403 if user is suspended."
weeks.pre_flight: Install bcryptjs (npm i bcryptjs @types/bcryptjs). Install express-session and connect-pg-simple (to store sessions in PostgreSQL) or iron-session for a cookie-only session. Know the Prisma schema for a User model with email (unique), passwordHash, role, and createdAt. Read the NextAuth documentation if you are in the Next.js path. Understand what an HttpOnly cookie is and why JavaScript cannot read it.
common_mistakes: Storing the full user object in the session instead of just the userId. If the user's role changes, the session still holds the old role. Always store the userId and re-fetch the user on each request (or use a short-lived cache).

Setting cookies without HttpOnly and Secure flags. HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie (blocks XSS token theft). Secure ensures the cookie is only sent over HTTPS. Both flags must be set in production. In development, Secure can be omitted for localhost.

Not expiring or rotating sessions after password changes. If a user changes their password, all existing sessions should be invalidated. Store a tokenVersion or passwordChangedAt on the user, increment it on password change, and validate it against the session on each request.

Logging passwords in error messages. If login fails and you log request bodies for debugging, passwords end up in your logs. Never log request bodies that may contain credentials. Redact sensitive fields from any logging middleware.

Using JWT for sessions without understanding the invalidation problem. If you use JWTs with a 24-hour expiry and a user is compromised, you cannot lock them out for 24 hours. Either use short-lived JWTs (15 minutes) with refresh tokens stored in the database, or just use sessions.
weeks.debug_help: Session cookie is not being sent on subsequent requests: check sameSite setting. If your frontend and backend are on different domains (localhost:3000 and localhost:4000), sameSite: 'none' and secure: true are required. In development with both on localhost, use sameSite: 'lax'. bcrypt.compare always returns false even with the correct password: you may be hashing the hash. Make sure you are storing the hash (the output of bcrypt.hash) and comparing against the original plain-text password. OAuth callback fails with "state mismatch": the state value was not stored before the redirect or was lost (e.g., session not initialised before the redirect). Ensure session middleware runs before the OAuth route. Google returns an error at the callback URL: check that your redirect URI in Google Cloud Console exactly matches the one you pass in the authorization URL — including trailing slashes and http vs https.
stretch: Implement refresh token rotation. Issue a short-lived JWT (15 min) and a long-lived refresh token stored in the database. On each use of the refresh token, issue a new pair and invalidate the old refresh token. This is more secure than a single long-lived JWT.

Add role-based access control. Users have roles: customer, staff, admin. Write middleware that accepts a required role and rejects requests from users with insufficient roles. Use it to protect admin-only endpoints.

Implement account lockout after 5 failed login attempts. Store failedLoginAttempts and lockedUntil on the User model. Increment on failure. Lock for 15 minutes after 5 failures. Reset on successful login.

weeks.title: Payments with Stripe — The Easy Way to Lose All Your Money
weeks.context:
Stripe is the standard for online payments because it handles the hard parts: PCI compliance, fraud detection, 3D Secure, global payment methods, tax calculation. Your job is to integrate it correctly — and "correctly" means understanding that webhooks, not API responses, are the source of truth.

Stripe primitives. A Customer is a Stripe object that represents a paying user — attach your user's database ID to the Stripe customer for lookups. A Product is what you sell (a SaaS plan, a physical item). A Price is how you sell it — attached to a Product, can be recurring (subscription) or one-time. A PaymentIntent represents an attempt to collect payment — it has a status lifecycle (requires_payment_method, requires_confirmation, processing, succeeded, canceled). A Subscription links a Customer to a Price with a billing cycle.

Checkout vs Elements. Stripe Checkout is a hosted payment page — Stripe renders the UI, handles card number entry, validation, and 3D Secure. Use Checkout for most apps: it is the fastest path to PCI compliance because card numbers never touch your server. Stripe Elements is a set of embeddable UI components — you control the layout, Stripe handles the secure input fields. Use Elements when you need a custom checkout experience (your design team will not accept the Stripe-hosted page).

Webhooks are the source of truth. When a user completes payment, Stripe fires a webhook to your server. You must handle these events and update your database accordingly — do not update the database based on the API response from your server-side checkout creation call, because the user might close the browser before the success page loads. The events you care about: checkout.session.completed, customer.subscription.created, customer.subscription.updated, customer.subscription.deleted, invoice.payment_succeeded, invoice.payment_failed. Verify webhook signatures using Stripe's library — reject any request that does not have a valid signature.

This week you add a subscription to Bean Forge. Users can subscribe to "Bean Forge Pro" for a monthly fee. You create the Stripe checkout session, handle the success/cancel redirects, and process webhooks to grant/revoke Pro status in your database.

Webhooks — why they're the source of truth, why signature verification matters
Idempotency keys — preventing double charges from network retries
Subscription lifecycle — trial, active, past_due, canceled — and what to do at each state
Refunds and disputes — partial vs full, chargebacks
Tax — Stripe Tax vs Paddle vs Merchant of Record
Testing — Stripe CLI, test cards, webhook forwarding

Build a Stripe Checkout integration that takes a payment for a one-time product
Build a subscription flow with a 7-day trial; verify the lifecycle events fire correctly
Implement webhook handling with signature verification + idempotency
Build a customer portal so users can cancel/upgrade subscriptions

Use Stripe Checkout for new subscriptions, the customer portal for managing existing ones. Webhook-driven entitlements: when subscription becomes active, the user's plan updates in your DB. Build a billing page that shows current plan + usage + an upgrade button. Test with the Stripe CLI before deploying.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user pays successfully, the Stripe Checkout redirect sends them to your /success page, and your success page marks them as Pro. What is the failure mode here? If the user closes the browser immediately after payment but before the redirect fires, your success page never loads, and the user is never marked as Pro. Stripe received the payment; your database does not know. The fix: never update the database based on a redirect. Instead, handle the checkout.session.completed webhook. Webhooks are server-to-server — they do not depend on the user's browser.

mastery_questions: A user pays successfully, the Stripe Checkout redirect sends them to your /success page, and your success page marks them as Pro. What is the failure mode here? If the user closes the browser immediately after payment but before the redirect fires, your success page never loads, and the user is never marked as Pro. Stripe received the payment; your database does not know. The fix: never update the database based on a redirect. Instead, handle the checkout.session.completed webhook. Webhooks are server-to-server — they do not depend on the user's browser.

Your webhook endpoint is receiving events. How do you verify that the request actually came from Stripe and is not a forged request from an attacker? Use stripe.webhooks.constructEvent(rawBody, signature, webhookSecret). The signature is in the Stripe-Signature header. Stripe signs the raw request body with your webhook secret. If you parse the body as JSON before calling constructEvent, the signature validation fails because the raw bytes have been altered. In Express, use express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) for the webhook route, not express.json().

A user's subscription is cancelled. What events does Stripe fire, and when does access end? When a subscription is cancelled, Stripe fires customer.subscription.updated with status "active" and cancel_at_period_end: true if it is a scheduled cancellation. At the end of the billing period, Stripe fires customer.subscription.deleted. You should revoke Pro access on the deleted event, not the updated event — the user has paid for access through the end of the period. Revoking early is a support ticket.

You want to offer a 14-day free trial before charging. How do you implement this with Stripe? Set the trial_period_days parameter when creating the subscription, or pass trial_end as a Unix timestamp. Stripe will not charge the customer until the trial ends. The subscription status during the trial is "trialing." You should still collect payment method upfront — otherwise many users will not add one before the trial ends. When the trial ends, Stripe fires customer.subscription.updated with status changing from "trialing" to "active."
ai_assist: "Write a Node.js/Express webhook handler for Stripe that handles checkout.session.completed, customer.subscription.updated, and customer.subscription.deleted. It should verify the signature, extract the relevant data, and update a Prisma User record with isPro and stripeSubscriptionId. Include idempotency: skip events that have already been processed."

"Write a TypeScript function that creates a Stripe Checkout session for a subscription. It takes userId and priceId, looks up or creates the Stripe Customer for that user, and returns the checkout URL. Include success and cancel URLs."
"Explain the Stripe payment status lifecycle for subscriptions: what events fire in what order for a new subscription, a successful renewal, a failed renewal, and a cancellation."
weeks.pre_flight: Create a Stripe account at stripe.com. Install the Stripe Node library: npm i stripe. Install the Stripe CLI for local webhook testing: stripe listen --forward-to localhost:4000/webhooks/stripe. Add STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, STRIPE_PRICE_ID (your Pro plan price ID) to your .env. Add a stripeCustomerId and isPro boolean to your User Prisma model. Read the Stripe docs quickstart for Node.js.
common_mistakes: Updating the database from the redirect URL instead of from webhooks. The redirect is a user experience signal, not a payment confirmation. Webhooks are the confirmation.

Parsing the webhook body with express.json() instead of express.raw(). The JSON parser transforms the raw bytes, breaking the HMAC signature verification. The webhook route must receive the raw body. Use express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) for that specific route.
Not verifying the webhook signature. If you skip verification, anyone can POST fake events to your webhook endpoint and grant themselves Pro access. Always verify.

Storing the Stripe secret key in your frontend code or git repository. The secret key can issue charges on your behalf. Store it in environment variables only, never in client-side code or in git history.

Not handling idempotency in webhook processing. Stripe may deliver the same webhook more than once. Your handler must be idempotent — processing the same event twice should not create two subscriptions. Use the Stripe event ID to track which events you have already processed.
weeks.debug_help: Webhook signature verification fails: check that you are using express.raw() not express.json() for the webhook route. Also verify the STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET matches the one shown in the Stripe CLI output when you run stripe listen. Checkout session creation fails with "No such price": the price ID in your .env does not match a real price in your Stripe account. Make sure you are using the correct mode — test mode prices start with price_ and are only visible in test mode. The Stripe CLI is not forwarding events: make sure you are running stripe listen --forward-to localhost:PORT/webhooks/stripe in a separate terminal. The webhook fires but the database is not updated: add console.log to your webhook handler to verify the event type matches what you are handling — the event object has a type field.
stretch: Add a customer portal link using Stripe Billing Portal. Users can manage their subscription (upgrade, downgrade, cancel) without you building any UI. One API call to create a portal session, redirect the user there.

Implement metered billing. Track usage in your application (e.g., number of API calls per month) and report it to Stripe using subscription items. Stripe bills based on the reported usage at the end of the billing period.

Handle failed payments. When invoice.payment_failed fires, send the user an email with a link to update their payment method. Give them 3 days before revoking access. Track payment failure state on the user model.

weeks.title: Email — Transactional, Marketing, and Why Your Inbox Hates You
weeks.context:
Email is infrastructure. When a user signs up, forgets their password, makes a purchase, or triggers any significant event, your application sends email. Getting email right means understanding the difference between transactional email and marketing email, the infrastructure that determines whether your message reaches the inbox, and the regulations that govern what you can send.

Transactional email is triggered by user action: welcome email, password reset, order confirmation, invoice. The user expects it. Send it from a transactional email provider: Resend, Postmark, or AWS SES. These providers optimise for deliverability on triggered, one-to-one messages.

Marketing email is bulk: newsletters, product announcements, promotional campaigns. Use a marketing email provider: Loops (good for SaaS), Mailchimp, or ConvertKit. The distinction matters because bulk email and transactional email have different sending patterns — ISPs treat them differently. Mixing them harms your transactional deliverability.

Deliverability: the science of getting email into the inbox. The three DNS records you must configure. SPF (Sender Policy Framework): a TXT record that lists the mail servers authorised to send email from your domain. Prevents strangers from sending email that appears to come from you. DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): your email provider generates a key pair. You publish the public key as a DNS TXT record. The provider signs outgoing emails with the private key. Recipients verify the signature. Proves the email was not altered in transit. DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance): a policy that tells receiving servers what to do with email that fails SPF and DKIM checks — reject it, quarantine it, or report it. Start with p=none (report only), move to p=quarantine, then p=reject.

Regulations. CAN-SPAM (US): all commercial email must include a physical mailing address and an unsubscribe link. The unsubscribe must work within 10 business days. GDPR (EU): you need consent to send marketing email to EU residents. Pre-ticked checkboxes do not count. Keep a record of when and how consent was given.

This week you add transactional email to Bean Forge: welcome email on signup, password reset flow (token generation, email dispatch, token verification), and order confirmation.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You send a password reset email with a token. The email contains a link to /reset-password?token=abc123. How do you implement this securely? Generate the token with crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex'). Hash it before storing in the database (use SHA-256 — it does not need to be bcrypt because password reset tokens are long-lived and random, not user-chosen). Store the hash, the userId it belongs to, and an expiry (15 minutes from now). Send the raw token in the email link. When the user clicks the link, hash the token from the URL, look up the hash in the database, verify it has not expired, then allow the password reset and delete the token. The reason you store the hash: if your database is breached, the attacker cannot use the stored tokens to reset passwords.

mastery_questions: You send a password reset email with a token. The email contains a link to /reset-password?token=abc123. How do you implement this securely? Generate the token with crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex'). Hash it before storing in the database (use SHA-256 — it does not need to be bcrypt because password reset tokens are long-lived and random, not user-chosen). Store the hash, the userId it belongs to, and an expiry (15 minutes from now). Send the raw token in the email link. When the user clicks the link, hash the token from the URL, look up the hash in the database, verify it has not expired, then allow the password reset and delete the token. The reason you store the hash: if your database is breached, the attacker cannot use the stored tokens to reset passwords.

A user reports they never received the welcome email. What do you check? First check your email provider dashboard for the send event — did it actually send? If yes, was it delivered? If delivered, ask the user to check spam/junk. If not delivered, check the bounce reason — invalid address, hard bounce (address does not exist) vs soft bounce (mailbox full). Check your sending domain's DNS records (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) using MX Toolbox. Check that the FROM address is from a verified domain. For transactional email, check that you are not sharing sending infrastructure with bulk senders.

You want to send an order confirmation email with a PDF attachment (the invoice). What does this look like in code with Resend? Resend accepts attachments as base64-encoded content. Generate the PDF using a library like PDFKit or @react-pdf/renderer. Convert the buffer to base64: buffer.toString('base64'). Pass it in the attachments array: [{ filename: 'invoice.pdf', content: base64String }]. The content-type is inferred from the filename or you can specify it explicitly with content_type: 'application/pdf'.

Your password reset tokens are stored in plain text in the database. A database breach occurs. What is the attacker able to do with these tokens? The attacker can use each valid token to reset the corresponding user's password and take over their account. This is why you hash the token before storing it. The token in the email is the raw random bytes — the database stores only the SHA-256 hash. Even with the hash, the attacker cannot reverse it to get the original token (tokens are 32 random bytes, not a dictionary word) and cannot use the hash as the token because the comparison is hash(incoming token) === stored hash.

Add a FROM_EMAIL to your .env (you can use onboarding@resend.dev in development without domain verification). Read the Resend Node.js quickstart. Know how to generate a cryptographically secure random token in Node: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex').
common_mistakes: Sending transactional email and marketing email from the same sending domain and infrastructure. If your newsletters get marked as spam, it damages the reputation of the domain and harms delivery of password reset emails. Use separate subdomains: mail.yourdomain.com for transactional, newsletter.yourdomain.com for marketing.

Not rate-limiting the password reset endpoint. Without rate limiting, an attacker can enumerate valid email addresses (by observing response time differences) or flood users with reset emails. Rate limit by IP and by email address.
Storing password reset tokens in plain text. If your database is breached, these are account takeover keys. Hash them with SHA-256 before storage.
Using non-expiring tokens. Password reset tokens must expire. 15 minutes for password reset, 24 hours for email verification. After use, delete the token immediately so it cannot be reused.

Not handling email bounces. If you keep sending to bounced addresses, your sender reputation suffers. Use your provider's webhook for bounce and complaint events to unsubscribe those addresses automatically.
weeks.debug_help: Resend returns a 403 error: your API key is wrong, or the FROM address is from a domain that is not verified in your Resend account. Check the email content — words like "FREE", "Click here", excessive punctuation trigger spam filters. Password reset link in email is wrong: check that your BASE_URL environment variable is set correctly and includes https:// without a trailing slash. The link is constructed as BASE_URL + '/reset-password?token=' + token. Email sends in development but not in production: check that RESEND_API_KEY is set in your production environment variables (not just .env).

weeks.title: File Uploads, Object Storage, and CDNs
weeks.context:
Storing files is not the same as storing data. Database rows are structured and indexed — they are designed for queries. Files are binary blobs that can be gigabytes. Storing them in your database (as BLOBs) works at small scale and is a mess at large scale. The standard architecture: store files in object storage, store the file metadata (URL, size, type, owner) in your database.

Object storage is the category. S3 is Amazon's implementation and the industry standard for the API. Every major cloud has an S3-compatible service: Cloudflare R2 (no egress fees, good choice for most apps), Backblaze B2, DigitalOcean Spaces, Google Cloud Storage. They all implement the same API. The Cloudflare R2 SDK is the AWS SDK with a different endpoint URL — the client code is identical.

Presigned URLs are the right way to handle uploads in a web application. The naive approach: browser uploads file to your server, your server uploads to S3. Problems: your server handles the bandwidth and compute cost, your server is in the critical path, large files can time out. The correct approach: browser asks your server for a presigned URL (a time-limited signed URL that allows a specific upload action), your server generates the presigned URL using the SDK, the browser uploads directly to S3 using that URL — your server is not in the upload path. Your server only handles metadata.

Image optimisation. Next.js has a built-in Image component that handles optimisation — it serves images in WebP or AVIF format (smaller than JPEG/PNG), resizes images to the displayed size (no serving a 2000px image in a 200px container), and lazy loads images below the fold. For user-uploaded images, you typically process them on the server after upload: resize to a maximum dimension, convert to WebP, generate thumbnail variants. Libraries: sharp (fast, native Node module).

Content Delivery Networks cache your static assets at edge locations close to your users. Without a CDN, every user downloads the original file from your single origin server, regardless of geography. With a CDN, the first request to each edge location fetches from origin and caches; subsequent requests are served from the edge — much faster for global audiences. Cloudflare R2 includes CDN functionality. AWS CloudFront sits in front of S3.

This week: add avatar upload to Bean Forge user profiles and menu item image upload to the admin panel using presigned URLs and Cloudflare R2.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Explain the presigned URL upload flow step by step, including what each party knows and does. Step 1: the browser asks your server for a presigned URL, sending the filename and content type. Step 2: your server validates the request (is the user authenticated? is the file type allowed?), generates a unique S3 key (e.g., users/userId/avatars/randomUUID.webp), calls S3 PutObjectCommand with the key and a 5-minute expiry to generate a presigned URL, and returns the URL and the final public URL of the file to the browser. Step 3: the browser makes a PUT request directly to S3 using the presigned URL, including the file bytes. The presigned URL encodes the allowed bucket, key, content type, and expiry — S3 verifies all of this. Step 4: after the upload succeeds, the browser tells your server the upload is complete, and your server updates the user's avatarUrl in the database to the public URL.

mastery_questions: Explain the presigned URL upload flow step by step, including what each party knows and does. Step 1: the browser asks your server for a presigned URL, sending the filename and content type. Step 2: your server validates the request (is the user authenticated? is the file type allowed?), generates a unique S3 key (e.g., users/userId/avatars/randomUUID.webp), calls S3 PutObjectCommand with the key and a 5-minute expiry to generate a presigned URL, and returns the URL and the final public URL of the file to the browser. Step 3: the browser makes a PUT request directly to S3 using the presigned URL, including the file bytes. The presigned URL encodes the allowed bucket, key, content type, and expiry — S3 verifies all of this. Step 4: after the upload succeeds, the browser tells your server the upload is complete, and your server updates the user's avatarUrl in the database to the public URL.

A user uploads a JPEG avatar. You want to: limit file size to 5MB, resize to 400x400, convert to WebP, and reject non-image files. How do you implement each constraint? File size: in your presigned URL generation, set the ContentLengthRange condition in a policy. Or enforce it client-side before requesting the URL (check file.size < 5 * 1024 * 1024). File type: check file.type on the client and the Content-Type in your server presigned URL request — only allow image/jpeg, image/png, image/webp, image/gif. Processing: after upload (triggered by a webhook from S3 or by a background job), download the file, run it through sharp with .resize(400, 400, { fit: 'cover' }).webp({ quality: 85 }), and replace the original in S3.

You are displaying 100 product images on a page. Each image is uploaded by an admin and stored at its original size (up to 5MB). What are the performance problems and how do you fix them? Problems: serving full-resolution images in small containers wastes bandwidth, browser must download 100 large files, no lazy loading means they all load at once. Fixes: serve resized variants (generate thumbnails on upload with sharp), use Next.js Image component which handles lazy loading and format optimisation, add Cache-Control headers to your S3 objects so the CDN caches them (max-age=31536000 for images that never change, shorter for images that might). Only the visible images should load initially — Next.js Image does this with loading="lazy".

An admin deletes a menu item. The menu item had an image in R2. What happens to the image? Nothing, unless you write code to delete it. S3 and R2 have no foreign key constraints — orphaned objects accumulate. Two approaches: delete the R2 object when the database record is deleted (synchronous, simple, can fail partway through and leave the database and storage out of sync); or use a background cleanup job that periodically scans for objects with no corresponding database record and deletes them (asynchronous, more robust). For most apps, the synchronous approach is fine with careful error handling.
ai_assist: "Write a Next.js API route that generates a presigned R2/S3 upload URL. It takes filename and contentType from the request body, validates that contentType is an image type, generates a unique key (users/{userId}/avatars/{uuid}.{ext}), creates a presigned PutObject URL with a 5-minute expiry, and returns both the presigned URL and the final public URL."

"Write a sharp-based image processing function that takes a Buffer (from S3 download), resizes it to 400x400 with cover cropping, converts it to WebP with 85% quality, and returns the processed Buffer."
"Write the CORS configuration JSON for Cloudflare R2 that allows PUT requests from localhost:3000 and my-production-domain.com, allows the Content-Type header, and exposes the ETag header."
weeks.pre_flight: Create a Cloudflare account and create an R2 bucket. Generate R2 API tokens (S3-compatible credentials). Install the AWS SDK S3 client: npm i @aws-sdk/client-s3 @aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner. Install sharp for image processing: npm i sharp. Add R2_ACCOUNT_ID, R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID, R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, R2_BUCKET_NAME, R2_PUBLIC_URL to your .env. Make sure your R2 bucket allows public access (for reading uploaded files).
common_mistakes: Uploading files through your server instead of using presigned URLs. For files larger than a few KB, your server becomes a bottleneck and files can time out on slow connections. Use presigned URLs to let the browser upload directly to storage.

Not validating file types on the server. A client-side check is a hint, not a security control. Validate the Content-Type in your presigned URL generation and verify the uploaded file's actual content (not just the MIME type header, which can be spoofed) using a library like file-type.

Storing file paths relative to your local filesystem instead of S3 URLs. If you store ./uploads/avatar.jpg, those files do not exist in production (Vercel, Railway, and similar platforms have ephemeral filesystems). Always store the full S3/R2 URL.

Setting Cache-Control headers that are too short (or not set at all) for static assets. Images that never change should have max-age=31536000, immutable. Without caching headers, every pageview re-fetches the same images.

Using the same S3 key for updated files. If a user uploads a new avatar and you store it at users/123/avatar.jpg (overwriting the old one), CDNs and browsers that cached the old URL will continue serving the old image. Use content-based keys (UUID or hash) so each upload has a unique URL.
weeks.debug_help: Presigned URL request returns "Access Denied": verify the R2 API token has read/write permissions for the bucket. Check that the bucket name in your code matches the actual bucket name. R2 returns a CORS error during upload: R2 buckets require CORS configuration. In your R2 bucket settings, add a CORS rule that allows PUT from your frontend domain with the Content-Type header. sharp fails to install: sharp is a native module that requires compilation. Run npm rebuild sharp after installing. On Windows, you may need the Visual Studio build tools. Alternatively, use sharp's WebAssembly build: npm i @img/sharp-wasm32. Uploaded images are accessible but show as broken: check that your R2 bucket is set to public access and that your R2_PUBLIC_URL environment variable matches the public URL shown in the R2 dashboard.
stretch: Add a blurhash placeholder for images. When an image is uploaded, generate a blurhash string using the blurhash library and store it with the image metadata. Display the blurhash as a blurred placeholder while the real image loads — this eliminates layout shift and gives a preview before the image arrives.

Implement image upload progress in the browser. Instead of using fetch for the presigned URL upload, use XMLHttpRequest — it has an upload.onprogress event that gives you bytes uploaded and total bytes. Show a progress bar to the user.

Set up S3 lifecycle rules on your bucket to automatically delete incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days. Large file uploads that are started but not completed leave partial data in S3 that costs money. Lifecycle rules clean this up automatically.

weeks.title: WebSockets and Real-time — When HTTP Isn't Enough
weeks.context:
HTTP is a request-response protocol: the client sends a request, the server sends a response, the connection is done. This model is fine for loading pages and submitting forms. It breaks down when you need the server to push data to connected clients — a live chat message, a real-time dashboard update, a collaborative editing change. For these use cases, you need WebSockets.

A WebSocket is a persistent, bidirectional connection between client and server. It starts as an HTTP connection (the handshake happens over HTTP), then upgrades to the WebSocket protocol. Once upgraded, both sides can send messages to each other at any time without the overhead of a new HTTP connection for each message. The connection stays open until either side closes it.

Socket.IO is the standard Node.js library for WebSockets. It wraps the WebSocket protocol with useful features: automatic reconnection when the connection drops, fallback to long-polling in environments that do not support WebSockets, rooms (named channels where you can broadcast to a subset of connected clients), and namespaces. The server emits events and clients listen for them; clients emit events and the server listens. The programming model is event-driven.

Scaling WebSockets is harder than scaling HTTP. HTTP servers are stateless — any server can handle any request. WebSocket connections are stateful — a connected client is connected to a specific server instance. If you have two server instances and clients connect to both, an event emitted on server 1 is not automatically sent to clients connected to server 2. The solution is an adapter: Socket.IO has a Redis adapter that routes messages between server instances via Redis pub/sub. In development with one server, this does not matter. In production, plan for it.

Server-Sent Events (SSE) are a simpler alternative for one-way server-to-client updates. SSE is a standard HTTP connection that the server keeps open and writes event data to periodically. The client uses the EventSource API. SSE is simpler than WebSockets (no library required, works over HTTP/2), but only supports server-to-client communication. For dashboards, notifications, and activity feeds, SSE is often the better choice.

This week you add real-time order status updates to Bean Forge. When an admin updates an order status, all customers watching that order see the update instantly.
