A paying customer wants to cancel their subscription. What is the ideal user experience and what happens technically on the Stripe side? The ideal UX: the user can cancel from their account settings page with one click (or via the Stripe Billing Portal). They see when their access ends (end of billing period). They get a cancellation confirmation email. Technically: your server calls stripe.subscriptions.update(subscriptionId, { cancel_at_period_end: true }). This sets the subscription to cancel at the end of the current period rather than immediately. The user retains access until then. When the period ends, Stripe fires customer.subscription.deleted and your webhook handler sets isPro: false on the user.

A potential employer looks at your Bean Forge GitHub repository. What should they see in the first 2 minutes? A clear README with: what the project is (one sentence), a live demo link, a screenshot or GIF, the tech stack, and how to set it up locally. Clean commit history (not "wip", "fix", "stuff" — real commit messages that describe what changed and why). Folder structure that makes sense (not everything in /src). A .env.example file with all required environment variables listed (values as placeholders). Tests that pass (link to CI badge). No secrets in the repository. The package.json should have useful scripts: dev, build, test, lint. This is a portfolio piece — it should show professional habits.

You decide to migrate Bean Forge from your PostgreSQL database to a new version with a schema change. The old Users table has a name column (VARCHAR). You want to split it into firstName and lastName. How do you do this without downtime? Step 1: add firstName and lastName columns (nullable). Step 2: deploy code that writes to all three columns and reads from firstName/lastName if they exist, falls back to name. Step 3: run a migration script to backfill firstName and lastName from name for all existing rows. Step 4: deploy code that only reads from firstName and lastName. Step 5: make name nullable (in case there are rows the backfill missed). Step 6: after verifying the new columns are correct, drop the name column. This sequence means no downtime because each step is backward compatible with the code deployed at the time.
ai_assist: "Write a production-ready README for a SaaS application called Bean Forge. Include: project description, live demo link placeholder, tech stack, local setup instructions (prerequisites, env setup, database setup, run), deployment guide for Vercel, and a contributing section."

"I'm preparing to launch on Product Hunt. Write a product description (tagline under 60 characters, description under 260 characters), three key features (each under 100 characters), and a comment I can post as the maker that tells the story of why I built this."

"Write an onboarding email sequence for Bean Forge: Day 0 (welcome, confirm email), Day 1 (how to add your first menu item), Day 3 (you can now take orders online), Day 7 (upgrade to Pro for analytics). Each email should be short (under 150 words), specific, and have one clear call to action."
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Your SaaS capstone audience is paying customers + investors + your future employer. They want: working product, real metrics, real revenue (even $1 is proof). Optimize for those three.
weeks.pre_flight: Buy a domain for Bean Forge (Namecheap or Cloudflare Registrar — Cloudflare's registrar charges at-cost with no markup). Connect it to Vercel. Set up SSL (Vercel handles this automatically). Create a Product Hunt account and draft a launch post. Write a README that explains what the project is, how to set it up locally, and how to deploy it. Add a CHANGELOG that lists major changes by week.
common_mistakes: Shipping without a real domain. localhost:3000 is not a portfolio project. A real domain costs $10/year. Without it, you cannot demonstrate SSL, CDN, production deployment, custom email from your domain, or any of the production setup work this course covered.

Leaving test/placeholder content in the production application. Bean Forge Pro should not have "TODO: write pricing copy" on the pricing page. Sweep the application for test data, placeholder text (Lorem Ipsum), disabled console.log statements left in, and debug routes.

No onboarding flow. When a new user signs up, they see a blank state and leave. An onboarding flow (even just an email sequence: welcome email day 1, "here's how to add your first menu item" day 2, "here are 5 things you can do" day 5) dramatically improves activation.

Skipping the README. A repository without a README is a repository that does not get hired. Write it as if a developer who knows nothing about your project must set it up from scratch. Then have someone actually try — the gaps will be obvious.

Not sharing the project. A portfolio project that no one knows about does not help your career. Post in communities. Tweet about it. Write a blog post about what you learned. The ability to build and distribute a product is what makes a developer employable — demonstrate both.
weeks.debug_help: Production site is slow after launch: first check where the slowness is — is it the server (time to first byte is slow, check your APM), the database (slow queries, add indexes), or the frontend (large bundle, missing CDN for images). Use WebPageTest.org to get a detailed breakdown from a real location. Domain not connecting to Vercel: check the DNS records. Vercel requires either an A record pointing to their IP (for apex domains) or a CNAME pointing to cname.vercel-dns.com. DNS changes take up to 48 hours to propagate — use dns.google to check current propagation status. Stripe webhooks not firing in production: check the Stripe dashboard under Developers > Webhooks — the endpoint must be configured for your production URL (not localhost). Check the event log for failed deliveries. Users cannot create accounts in production: check that all required environment variables are set in Vercel (DATABASE_URL, NEXTAUTH_SECRET, etc.) and that the production database is accessible from Vercel's edge network.
stretch: Write a retrospective document. Looking back at 24 weeks: what was the hardest week and why? What would you do differently if you started over? What are you most proud of in the code? What technical debt exists that you would address next? This exercise builds engineering judgment — the ability to evaluate your own work critically is what separates junior from senior developers.

Open source Bean Forge on GitHub with an MIT license. Write a CONTRIBUTING.md guide. See if you can get one external contribution (a bug fix, a documentation improvement) from someone who found the project. Responding to an external PR — reviewing it, suggesting changes, merging it — is a skill most bootcamp graduates lack.

Submit Bean Forge to three public curated lists or directories: Product Hunt, Indie Hackers, and one relevant community subreddit. Track signups from each source using UTM parameters (/?utm_source=producthunt&utm_campaign=launch). After one week, look at which source drove the most signups. This is growth thinking applied to your own product.
